books.summary: A very well written book on the great crash of 1929. It is really quite remarkable how similar those times were to the current age. Apparently Sorkin wrote this after he wrote about the 2008 Financial Crisis because he was so struck by the fact that we hadn't learned from the mistakes of 1929. And it feels like we haven't learned from the mistakes of 2008 either.

books.title: 21 Lessons for the 21st Century
books.summary: 21 Lessons for the 21st Century surveys the major political, technological, social, and existential challenges facing humanity today. Harari groups his analysis into themes such as the disruptive impact of artificial intelligence and biotechnology on jobs and human identity, the erosion of liberal democracy, the rise of nationalism and populism, and the dangers of misinformation and terrorism. He also addresses global threats like climate change, nuclear war, and the fragility of truth in a digital age. The book argues that traditional narratives—religion, nationalism, even liberal humanism—struggle to provide meaning in this new era. Harari concludes that cultivating clarity, resilience, and ethical awareness, especially through meditation and critical thinking, is essential for individuals and societies to navigate an uncertain future.

books.title: A Brief History of Intelligence
books.summary: A Brief History of Intelligence traces the evolutionary journey of human intelligence through five foundational breakthroughs—from early steering behaviors in nematodes, to reinforcement learning in vertebrates, simulation in mammals via the neocortex, social mentalizing in primates, and finally to the emergence of speech in humans. Bennett argues that these milestones—rooted in biology over hundreds of millions of years—can illuminate how and why contemporary AI systems both mimic and fall short of human cognition. While AI has achieved remarkable feats like game mastery and pattern recognition, human brains continue to outperform machines in flexible, context-sensitive, sequential learning and imagination. The book underscores that a true understanding of natural intelligence, as revealed through its evolutionary arc, is essential for guiding the development of genuinely intelligent AI systems—and prompts us to consider AI’s future impact on humanity.

books.title: A Dominant Character
books.summary: A Dominant Character is a vivid biography of J. B. S. Haldane, the brilliant, boisterous, and polarising geneticist whose life straddled groundbreaking science and radical politics. Subramanian portrays Haldane’s early experiences—from a childhood shaped by his scientist father’s experiments, to serving in the trenches of World War I and conducting self-experiments on his own body—as crucial to his fearless curiosity. Haldane's scientific achievements include foundational work in population genetics (linkage, mutation rates, heterozygote advantage, evolutionary theory) and prescient predictions in his 1924 book about future technologies—from IVF to renewable energy. Yet, his unwavering commitment to Communism led him into moral conflict, notably during the Lysenko affair, where he sided with political loyalty over scientific integrity. His later years saw him move to India, embracing its academic landscape while retaining his candidness and vigour. Subramanian neither lionises nor condemns him, instead compassionately revealing Haldane’s intellectual contradictions, flamboyant style, and enduring relevance to debates on science, belief, and the public role of scientists.

books.title: A Part Apart
books.summary: A sweeping, deeply researched biography of B.R. Ambedkar that traces the arc of his life alongside the evolution of his thought, drawing on both Marathi and English sources long neglected by earlier accounts. Far from hagiography, Gopal presents Ambedkar as a complex figure, examining his scholarship, his campaigns against caste, and his disagreements with Gandhi, Tilak, the Hindu Mahasabha, and the communists over the path to social reform.

books.title: A Promised Land
books.summary: A Promised Land_ is Barack Obama’s introspective memoir that chronicles his journey from community organizer to the presidency, focusing on his early life, political awakening, 2008 campaign, first term’s defining moments—like the financial crisis recovery, passage of the Affordable Care Act, and the mission that led to Osama bin Laden’s death—and his struggles with leadership, race, intimacy, and hope. Obama aims to offer an honest window into what it means to be president, exploring both policy and personal dimensions—marital strains, self-doubt, and the weight of history—while holding onto a narrative of democracy, resilience, and progress.

books.title: A Sixth of Humanity
books.summary: A wide-ranging account of independent India's development, arguing that the country attempted four simultaneous transformations—building a state, an economy, a society, and a sense of nationhood—all under universal suffrage from the outset. Kapur and Subramanian characterise the resulting model as "precocious," with democracy and a service economy arriving ahead of industrialisation, and describe the trajectory as one of prolonged ruralisation, stunted industrialisation, and premature servicification.

books.title: AI Snake Oil
books.summary: A clear-eyed guide to telling genuine artificial intelligence from hype, written by computer scientists Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor. They distinguish the real advances in generative AI from the predictive systems—used in hiring, lending, and criminal justice—that they argue frequently do not and cannot work as advertised, while also examining the flaws of the technology that does function.

books.title: AI Super-Powers
books.summary: AI Superpowers analyzes the global AI competition between the United States and China, arguing that China has rapidly closed the AI gap due to its vast data access, bold startup culture, limited data regulation, and government backing. Lee explains that AI development now hinges less on groundbreaking ideas and more on scaling—processing immense amounts of data, leveraging abundant computing power, and mobilizing numerous engineers. He outlines how AI threatens both white-collar and blue-collar jobs in structured, routine roles but leaves social, creative, and empathetic professions—like caregiving and therapy—relatively safer. The book concludes that while AI offers transformative potential, society must proactively manage its risks through adaptation, regulation, and a human-centered approach to ensure technology enhances rather than diminishes our future.

books.title: AIQ
books.summary: AIQ: How People and Machines Are Smarter Together explains how artificial intelligence works by translating its mathematical foundations—like probability, regression, Bayes' rule, language processing, and anomaly detection—into accessible, story-driven lessons. Each chapter begins with a historical anecdote, from WWII statistics to pioneering researchers, before linking those ideas to modern applications like recommendation systems, personalized medicine, and AI-powered diagnostics. The authors aim to equip readers with enough understanding to engage meaningfully in AI debates, balancing optimism about AI's potential with awareness of its limitations and societal impacts.

books.title: Aadhaar - A Biometric History of India's 12-Digit Revolution
books.summary: Aadhaar traces the birth and evolution of the Aadhaar biometric identity system, launched in 2009 under Nandan Nilekani’s leadership, designed to use biometrics and demographics to deliver social welfare more efficiently, curb corruption, and save public funds. Journalist Shankkar Aiyar narrates how the project gained bipartisan political support despite ideological differences, and how its applications expanded far beyond welfare—including banking, telecom, and government services. He recounts the system’s rapid enrollment and growing pains, critiques over surveillance and privacy threats, and makes the case for a robust data‑protection law. The book is both a dramatic chronicle of India’s recent political and technological transformation and a probing reflection on the trade-offs between inclusion and civil liberties.

books.title: Accelerating India’s Development
books.summary: Accelerating India’s Development argues that India’s slow progress in public service delivery—such as education, health, public safety, justice, and jobs—is not due to lack of spending but stems from weak state capacity, including poor data systems, under-resourced bureaucracy, and rigid centralization. Muralidharan shows that while the state can succeed in “mission-mode” tasks like elections or vaccination campaigns, it fails in daily service delivery. He offers data-driven, evidence-based reforms such as performance-linked incentives, hiring locally on renewable contracts, stronger data infrastructure, decentralization, and better state-market coordination to ensure public goods reach citizens efficiently, equitably, and at scale. The book’s central message is that India must strengthen its institutional capacity to convert growth into real human development—and this is the vital unfinished task of Indian democracy.

books.title: Accidental Feminism
books.summary: Accidental Feminism sets out to understand the treatment of gender in elite Indian law firms and discovers, almost to the author's surprise, remarkable levels of gender parity—even though they make no deliberate feminist commitment. Drawing on interviews with over 130 professionals across transactional law and consulting, Ballakrishnen identifies four key factors behind this phenomenon: gender frames (the fact that newer firms lack entrenched gendered blueprints, offering women more equitable access); speculative isomorphism (firms emulate global modernity unconsciously favoring meritocratic representations, including women); client facings (female lawyers provide emotional and relational value in deal-making contexts, enhancing their professional worth); and family support (intergenerational support structures empower women to ascend to leadership). These advantages generate visibly egalitarian outcomes, but since they came about without institutional intent, they remain fragile and hard to replicate more broadly across society.

books.title: Age of Revolutions
books.summary:
In "Age of Revolutions: Progress and Backlash from 1600 to the Present," Fareed Zakaria examines transformative periods in history to shed light on contemporary global challenges. He identifies three pivotal historical revolutions:

1. **The Dutch Golden Age (17th Century):** Zakaria explores how the Netherlands' unique geographic and political conditions fostered a liberal state that prioritized trade, innovation, and religious tolerance, setting the stage for modern democratic governance.  

2. **The French Revolution (Late 18th Century):** He analyzes the tumultuous events in France, highlighting how abrupt ideological shifts led to instability and violence, offering lessons on the complexities of rapid societal change. 

3. **The Industrial Revolution:** Zakaria discusses the technological advancements that began in Great Britain and later spread to the United States, transforming economies and societies, and leading to both progress and significant social upheaval.

Building on these historical insights, Zakaria addresses four contemporary revolutions:

1. **Globalization:** He examines the unprecedented level of global economic interdependence, which has led to both economic growth and widespread anxiety due to rapid changes and job displacement. 

2. **Technological Advancement:** Zakaria delves into the digital revolution, noting how information technology has reshaped economies and societies, bringing about both opportunities and challenges. 

3. **Identity Politics:** He explores the rise of identity-based movements, emphasizing how cultural and social transformations have led to new political alignments and conflicts. 

4. **Geopolitical Shifts:** Zakaria analyzes the changing dynamics of global power, particularly the challenges to the liberal international order posed by emerging powers and shifting alliances. 

Throughout the book, Zakaria emphasizes the cyclical nature of progress and backlash, suggesting that understanding these patterns is crucial for navigating the current era of rapid change.

books.title: Air-Borne
books.summary: A history of aerobiology and of the air itself as a living medium, tracing how scientists came to understand that the atmosphere teems with microbes, spores, pollen, and viruses. Zimmer weaves the long, often-ignored science of airborne life with the story of how that neglect shaped the response to COVID-19, and how hard-won recognition of airborne transmission finally arrived.

books.title: Algorithms to Live By
books.summary:
A book about applying algorithmic principles and computational thinking to everyday life. It encourages readers to approach their personal development with the same structured, analytical mindset as programmers design efficient code. It suggests that algorithms, which are step-by-step procedures for solving problems, can be analogous tools for self-improvement and discusses how systematic strategies and logical approaches can optimize daily routines, enhance productivity, and foster personal growth.

It uses computational concepts like those in machine learning to understand human learning processes, emphasizing adaptability, and the importance of continuous learning providing actionable strategies for setting goals and making decisions, leveraging the power of structure and order to enhance life quality.

books.title: An Immense World
books.summary: An Immense World** argues that every animal—including humans—experiences only a tiny slice of reality, as defined by its own sensory bubble or “Umwelt.” Yong explores a wide array of sensory abilities—dogs tracking scents, turtles sensing magnetic fields, fish detecting electricity, scallops with hundreds of rudimentary eyes, birds distinguishing song elements humans miss—and shows how each species perceives a unique world. He emphasizes that the world is far richer than humans can sense, uses vivid examples from nature, and warns that human sensory pollution—light, noise, chemical interference—is disrupting these delicate perceptual worlds. The book’s core message: to truly understand and protect life on Earth, we must acknowledge and value the hidden sensory realms of other species.

books.title: Anaximander
books.summary: "Anaximander" argues that this pre-Socratic Greek philosopher from the 6th century BCE was not only one of our first true scientists but also initiated a profound intellectual revolution that shaped the development of scientific thinking. Anaximander made the revolutionary leap of suggesting that the Earth floats in space supported by nothing, rejected supernatural explanations for natural phenomena, and introduced the concept that natural laws, not gods, govern the universe. It was this radical departure from mythological thinking to naturalistic explanation - this ability to imagine a reality different from immediate appearances and this introduction of scientific abstraction that represents the true birth of scientific thought, making him a crucial figure in the history of human knowledge whose conceptual breakthrough continues to influence how we understand the world today.

books.title: Antisocial Media
books.summary: Antisocial Media argues that Facebook’s rise stemmed from hubristic ideals of connection, but the platform has devolved into a powerful engine of surveillance capitalism that erodes democracy and civil discourse. Vaidhyanathan explores how Facebook manipulates attention through emotionally charged content, traps users with addictive feedback loops, and reduces the information ecosystem to chaotic, emotionally-driven noise. The platform amplifies tribalism, filter bubbles, and targeted persuasion—enabling manipulation in politics, disinformation, and social division. Vaidhyanathan concludes that the core problem isn’t a flaw or misuse, but is structural: “the problem with Facebook is Facebook,” and surface-level fixes can’t undo its deep political and cultural impact. He advocates for strong privacy and antitrust measures—like breaking up the company—but remains skeptical about their sufficiency without deeper systemic change.

books.title: Army of None
books.summary: Army of None examines the rise of lethal autonomous weapons—machines capable of targeting and killing without human orders—and the profound military, legal, and moral dilemmas they raise. Scharre, drawing on his experience as a U.S. Army Ranger and Pentagon defence strategist, defines key differences between automated and autonomous systems, illustrates how technologies like Aegis and Harpy already exhibit partial autonomy, and explores how AI advances may enable fully independent weaponry. He questions whether machines can navigate moral choices—such as sparing a child who may be a threat—and warns that removing humans from the loop risks accidental escalation and unlawful violence. The book surveys the global race for autonomous arms, considers whether bans are feasible, and ultimately calls for safeguards—such as bans on antipersonnel autonomous weapons, clear norms requiring meaningful human control, and international rules—to ensure that the precision and speed of machines don’t override human judgment in life-or-death decisions.

books.title: Aroused
books.summary: Aroused offers a lively, accessible history of hormones—chemical messengers essential for everything from metabolism, mood, and sleep to reproduction, stress, and immunity. Epstein traces the origins of endocrinology from early experiments (like transplanting testicles in roosters) to modern hormone therapies, weaving together stories of pioneering scientists, medical breakthroughs, and unscrupulous quacks. Through anecdotes about figures such as Harvey Cushing, Rosalyn Yalow, and various hormone-driven quack remedies—from libido-boosting vasectomies to “liquid trust”—she reveals how hormones have been both life-saving and misunderstood. Ultimately, the book demystifies the endocrine system, illustrating both its profound influence on human life and the cultural, medical, and scientific hype that has shaped our understanding of these invisible forces in our bodies.

books.title: Assembling India's Constitution
books.summary: A revisionist history of how India's constitution was made, shifting the focus away from the Constituent Assembly to the ordinary people who shaped it from below. Drawing on an extraordinary archive of petitions, resolutions, and records from civic associations, marginalised groups, universities, and religious bodies, De and Shani show that constitution-making unfolded as a broad public process, with citizens turning constitutionalism into a medium of struggle.

books.title: Astrophysics for People in a Hurry
books.summary: Astrophysics for People in a Hurry is a concise introduction to the universe and humanity’s place within it. Tyson explains the Big Bang and cosmic expansion, the formation of galaxies and stars, the role of dark matter and dark energy, and the elements that make life possible. He explores the physics of light, gravity, and the space-time fabric, while also reflecting on exoplanets, black holes, and the search for extraterrestrial life. The book balances scientific explanation with philosophical reflection, emphasizing that the cosmos is vast, mysterious, and interconnected, and that understanding it not only satisfies curiosity but also offers perspective on our responsibilities as inhabitants of a fragile planet.

books.title: Becoming Leonardo
books.summary: Lankford strips away the myths surrounding Leonardo da Vinci to reconstruct him as a flawed, intense, and deeply curious human. Drawing on archival details and vivid speculation, he portrays Leonardo as a solitary figure whose illegitimate birth, brushes with poverty, fleeting patronage, and brushes with scandal influenced his relentless independence and creative restlessness. Set against the sensory-rich backdrop of Renaissance Italy—marked by war, plague, intrigue, and artistic rivalry—the biography shows Leonardo fleeing sanctuary to sanctuary, surviving through ingenuity, and perpetually abandoning commissions in pursuit of understanding. Lankford’s speculative reconstruction emphasises Leonardo’s humanity—his failures, fears, and improvisational genius—offering an intimate, unconventional, and thought-provoking portrait of the elusive Renaissance master.

books.title: Being Mortal
books.summary: Being Mortal argues that modern medicine, while adept at prolonging life, often fails those facing ageing and death by focusing on survival rather than well-being. Gawande shares personal stories—from his own family members to patients in retirement homes—and reveals how facilities prioritising safety can strip away autonomy and dignity. He explores alternatives like assisted living designed to preserve freedom, and hospice care that centres on comfort and meaning. The core message is that end-of-life care should shift from extending time to enriching it—prioritising what individuals value most and enabling them to live with purpose and control until the very end.

books.title: Bird by Bird
books.summary: Part writing manual, part memoir on the writing life, offering practical craft advice alongside candid reflection on self-doubt, perfectionism, and persistence. The title comes from Lamott's father's advice to a panicked child facing a huge school report—to take it "bird by bird"—and stands for her core counsel to work in small pieces and tolerate the "shitty first draft."

books.title: Blue
books.summary: Blue is a globe-trotting exploration into humanity’s fascination with the colour blue—one of the rarest hues in nature. Kupferschmidt follows his lifelong obsession across continents and disciplines, from the accidental discovery of a vibrant new pigment (YInMn blue) to the complexities behind blue in nature—from butterflies and flowers to crystals and the sky. He unpacks how blue has been treasured by ancient civilisations, its chemical and structural underpinnings, and its elusive presence in plants, animals, and even food. The book blends science, culture, history, and personal reflection to reveal how blue—so visually pervasive yet chemically rare—connects us to nature’s beauty, fragility, and mystery.

books.title: Born a Muslim
books.summary: Born a Muslim is a deeply personal and meticulously reported exploration of what it means to be Muslim in contemporary India. Ghazala Wahab combines memoir, history, reportage, and analysis to trace the journey from the early origins of Islam to its arrival in the subcontinent, the impact of Partition, and the structural discrimination and persistent prejudices faced by Indian Muslims today. Through vivid stories and candid reflection, she reveals how insecurity and marginalisation are woven into the lived realities of the community, while also reminding us of their agency, diversity, and resilience. The book challenges stereotypes, promotes nuanced understanding, and underscores the urgent need for empathy and inclusive dialogue in India's public sphere.

books.title: Boundary Lab
books.summary: Boundary Lab argues that organised sport functions as a “petri dish” where societies prototype rules, markets and morals before they spill into the wider world. Drawing on Indian and global cases, Nandan Kamath traces how disputes over autonomy and governance, integrity (doping, corruption, match-fixing), inclusion and difference, technological innovation, valuation and broadcasting, and the ever-precarious balance between player rights, commercial incentives and public interest are worked out inside sport’s bounded arena.

books.title: Breakneck
books.summary: An on-the-ground account of China’s tumultuous decade under Xi Jinping, chronicling how the country’s economic model shifted from digital consumer innovation to state-driven industrial and technological self-reliance. Drawing from his years living and working in China, Wang argues that while the West fixated on China’s tech giants and censorship, the real transformation occurred in factories, supply chains, and industrial policy — where China built world-class capabilities in batteries, semiconductors, and advanced manufacturing. He portrays a society caught between confidence in its productive capacity and fear of political tightening, exploring how the state’s push for control reshaped entrepreneurship, education, and daily life. The book concludes that China’s future will depend less on consumer apps and more on whether it can sustain innovation under authoritarian constraint — a balance that defines both its success and fragility.

books.title: Burn Book
books.summary: A memoir-manifesto that traces the career of one of Silicon Valley’s most influential and feared journalists, while also providing a sharp critique of the tech industry’s culture and excesses. Swisher recounts her early days covering the rise of the internet, her relationships with powerful figures like Steve Jobs, Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, and Jeff Bezos, and how the industry shifted from idealistic innovation to monopolistic dominance and reckless pursuit of power. She blends personal anecdotes with reporting to expose how arrogance, lack of accountability, and disregard for consequences shaped today’s digital giants, while reflecting on her own role in both chronicling and shaping the tech narrative.

books.title: Caged Tiger
books.summary:
"Caged Tiger: How Too Much Government Is Holding Indians Back" by Subhashish Bhadra examines how India's institutional frameworks, many rooted in the colonial era, continue to impede individual freedoms and societal progress. Bhadra argues that despite India's political independence, remnants of colonial governance persist, leading to overregulation and constraints on citizens.*

*The book delves into various sectors where excessive governmental control is evident:*

- **Economic Policies:** *interventions such as subsidies and price controls, often hinder economic efficiency and growth*. 
- **Civil Liberties:** *issues like surveillance, censorship, and restrictions on free speech stifle democratic expression.* 
- **Law Enforcement:** *there is a need for police reforms, because outdated systems contribute to inefficiencies and injustices.* 
- **Cultural Restrictions:** *There are legal limitations on cultural expressions, censorship in media and arts, and regulations affecting personal choices.* 
- **Legislative Challenges:** *India's legislative bodies function poorly with issues like disruptions, lack of accountability, and the influence of money in politics.* 

*Throughout "Caged Tiger," Bhadra emphasizes the importance of institutional reforms to unlock India's potential, advocating for a balance between necessary governance and individual freedoms.

books.title: Careless People
books.summary: Careless People is a first-person memoir by a former Facebook/Meta public-policy executive that traces how the company’s growth-at-all-costs culture, executive impunity, and PR-driven decision-making warped its handling of crises from Myanmar to teen mental health and China outreach. It recounts internal battles over content moderation and integrity, describes alleged sexual harassment and retaliation dynamics, and details how leadership prioritized metrics, market access, and optics over safety, transparency, and accountability. Threading personal experience with contemporaneous documents and media scrutiny, it shows how lofty mission language masked a pattern of expediency—under-resourcing non-English trust and safety, bending rules for powerful actors, and exploring censorship-enabling compromises abroad—culminating in legal attempts to silence the author. The book’s conclusion is that these were not isolated missteps but features of an incentives system that rewarded deniability and growth, requiring external oversight and structural reform rather than promises of self-regulation.

books.title: Chaos Monkeys
books.summary: Chaos Monkeys is a candid, irreverent insider’s account of the chaos, ambition, and ruthlessness of Silicon Valley. García Martínez recounts his journey from Wall Street to co-founding a startup, its chaotic acquisition by Twitter, and later his turbulent stint at Facebook. Along the way, he exposes the vanity, greed, politics, and raw power struggles that define the tech industry, where billion-dollar decisions are made amid constant uncertainty and inflated promises. Mixing memoir with sharp critique, the book portrays Silicon Valley as a place of immense innovation but also hubris and dysfunction, where disruptive technology is inseparable from the messy, flawed humans who create it.

books.title: China’s Drive for the Technology Frontier
books.summary: Rather technical book on China and how it drove its technology policy to become world beating. Interestign perspective if you read this along with Dan Wang's Breakneck. This is a much more sober and pro-China take but the decades long push to achieve technological superiority is clear to see.

books.title: Co-Intelligence
books.summary: Co-Intelligence argues that in the age of AI—especially generative models like ChatGPT—we should view artificial intelligence not as a threat, but as a “co-intelligence”: a versatile partner that amplifies human capabilities. Mollick outlines four core principles to guide our collaboration: invite AI into all tasks to learn its strengths and limits; always remain the human in the loop to ensure oversight and judgment; treat AI like a person by giving it clear roles and context; and recognise that today’s AI is only the beginning—it’s the worst we’ll ever use. He shows how AI can act as a creative collaborator, tutor, coworker, and coach, reshaping education, workplace productivity, and creative practice. Mollick also presents four possible futures—ranging from slow, manageable AI growth to exponential advances culminating in superintelligent systems—encouraging proactive, thoughtful engagement today to shape an AI-augmented tomorrow.

books.title: Code and Other Laws of Cyberspace
books.summary: A foundational work of internet law arguing that in cyberspace "code is law"—that the software and hardware architecture of the digital world regulates behaviour as powerfully as any statute. Lessig warns that the early internet's openness was not inevitable and that commercial and governmental pressures could quietly re-engineer it toward control, making the case that we must consciously choose the values we build into the network.

books.title: Congress Radio
books.summary: Congress Radio recounts how 22-year-old student activist Usha Mehta and her collaborators established an underground radio station—Congress Radio—during the 1942 Quit India Movement to broadcast uncensored news and speeches from leaders like Gandhi. Operating from shifting locations in Bombay using secret transmitters, the station provided a vital counter-narrative to British-controlled media and galvanised the independence movement. Despite technical challenges, the prison-like secrecy, and the eventual betrayal of insiders, the radio’s symbolic power resonated even after it was shut down. Arrested after months on air, Mehta’s bravery, defiance during trial, and the legacy of the broadcasts cemented her place as a key, though often overlooked, figure in India's struggle for freedom.

books.title: Connections
books.summary: Connections explores how seemingly unrelated discoveries, innovations, and historical events are intertwined in unexpected ways to shape the modern world. Burke traces chains of cause and effect across time and disciplines—showing, for example, how a seemingly obscure invention or accident set off a domino effect leading to pivotal scientific breakthroughs, cultural shifts, or technological revolutions. Through engaging stories that weave together invention, exploration, and human curiosity, the book reveals how progress is seldom linear, but rather a complex web of connections—urging readers to see the world not as isolated facts but as a richly interlinked tapestry.

books.title: Conspiracy - A True Story of Power, Sex, and a Billionaire’s Secret Plot to Destroy a Media Empire
books.summary: Conspiracy chronicles how Peter Thiel orchestrated a nearly decade-long secret campaign to destroy Gawker Media after it outed him as gay in a blog post. Thiel covertly bankrolled Hulk Hogan’s lawsuit over the publication of a sex tape, using the courts to bring about Gawker’s bankruptcy and shuttering the site with a $140 million judgment. Ryan Holiday decrypts the layers of planning, strategy, and moral complexity behind the scheme—highlighting how power, patience, and secrecy can tilt battles and reshape media, privacy, and justice in the modern age.

books.title: Conspiracy- A History of Bollocks Theories, and How Not to Fall for Them
books.summary: This book explores the strange, entertaining, and often troubling history of conspiracy theories—from moon landing denial and the Satanic Panic to QAnon and anti-vaccine movements—arguing that humans are continually drawn to believing we're being deceived, even when the truth is plain. Phillips and Elledge take readers through bizarre backstories such as UFO sightings, rumours about Britney Spears, and claims that centuries of European history might be fabricated. Blending humour with serious insight, they warn that indulging in conspiratorial thinking can erode trust in evidence and institutions, and challenge readers to abandon online echo chambers in favour of scepticism grounded in hard facts.

books.title: Court on Trial
books.summary:
A critical exploration of the Indian Supreme Court's functioning, based on empirical data and rigorous analysis. The authors delve into the court’s institutional framework, workload, decision-making processes, and its ability to deliver justice in a timely and effective manner.*

*It uncovers systemic inefficiencies, structural challenges, and discrepancies between the court’s ideals and its reality. These include issues like delays in case resolution, inconsistent jurisprudence, and an ever-expanding docket that strains the court's capacity. The court’s procedural rules and institutional design affect its accessibility, equity, and overall effectiveness. Additionally, certain structural and administrative practices, such as the role of the Chief Justice in determining benches, influence outcomes and public trust. It raises critical questions about the balance between judicial activism and judicial restraint, and whether the court is meeting its constitutional mandate or veering into areas best left to the legislature and executive.*

*It provides a clear, evidence-based understanding of the Supreme Court’s institutional performance based on statistical analysis and case studies.

books.title: Cult of the Dead Cow
books.summary: The story of cDc, one of the most influential and longest-running hacker groups in American history, emerging from Lubbock, Texas, in the 1980s and evolving from prankster tech enthusiasts into ethical pioneers of hacktivism. Menn recounts how they invented the concept of hacktivism, created tools like Back Orifice to expose security flaws, and launched movements like Hacktivismo to defend free expression online. Along the way, members influenced cybersecurity policy at the highest levels, helped shape privacy projects like Tor, and built a legacy of activism and moral reflection in the internet age. Drawing from in-depth reporting and personal profiles, the book shows how mischievous outsiders eventually became "graybeards"—trusted advisors to governments and tech organisations—and argues that their blend of technical audacity and ethical purpose offers invaluable lessons for steering technology toward the public good.

books.title: Dangerous Miracle
books.summary: A natural and social history of antibiotics by biologist Liam Shaw, spanning the deep evolutionary origins of these compounds and the past century of their medical use. Shaw explains how antibiotic development became commercially unattractive, how patents and regulation skew research away from urgent need, and why a rising tide of resistance—alongside gaps in access—threatens to squander one of medicine's greatest gifts.

books.title: Deep Medicine
books.summary: In Deep Medicine, Eric Topol argues that modern healthcare has become “shallow”—doctors overwhelmed by documentation, diagnostic overload, and burnout end up spending less time with patients. He shows how AI—especially deep learning—can absorb routine tasks, analyse scans, and sift through vast clinical data, enabling doctors to reclaim empathy, focus, and presence. Topol illustrates how AI systems already outperform clinicians in areas like image-based diagnoses and disease prediction, while also reducing misdiagnoses and unnecessary procedures. The book advocates for a healthcare model where technology serves to augment human judgment and compassionate care—not replace it—paving the way for a more humane and effective medical practice.

books.title: Delhi Reborn
books.summary: Delhi Reborn explores how the twin upheavals of Partition and independence transformed Delhi from the late 1930s through the mid-1950s. Geva examines the ways in which nationalist visions—like those for Pakistan—were first nurtured in the city’s interwar cultural and intellectual life, then brutally territorialized as violence and displacement reshaped neighborhoods and altered social geography. She brings into focus the erosion of Muslim security, the instrumental roles of figures like Patel and Nehru in shaping state responses, and the decline of the Urdu public sphere even as it once served to articulate belonging and resistance. Grounded in rich archival research, microhistories, and evocative literary and journalistic voices, the book shows how Delhi became both a symbol and a staging ground for nation-building, reflecting the tension between democratic aspirations and authoritarian imperatives—and how those unresolved tensions continue to echo in contemporary urban and political India.

books.title: Dent's Modern Tribes
books.summary: Dent’s Modern Tribes is a playful and insightful exploration of the hidden vocabularies of British “tribes”—from taxi drivers and emergency-room medics to trainspotters, bankers, and cabin crew—revealing how each group uses its own secret language to bond, exclude, and communicate efficiently. Susie Dent collected these distinctive terms and phrases through interviews and keen eavesdropping, showcasing how jargon, slang, acronyms, and coded humour both reflect and reinforce group identity. Whether it's “jack brew” (a solo cuppa) among soldiers, “UBI” (unexplained beer incident) in hospital halls, or “slam-clicker” for cabin crew who vanish straight to hotels, the book offers a whirlwind phrasebook of Britain’s society—with wit, history, and a tribute to the hidden lexicons we all inhabit.

books.title: Digital Empires
books.summary:
An analysis of how the United States, China, and the European Union are shaping the future of the digital economy through distinct regulatory models.* 

- **American Market-Driven Model**: This model emphasizes minimal government intervention, prioritizing free markets and innovation. Tech companies largely set the rules, fostering rapid growth but also leading to concerns about data privacy and market concentration.
- **Chinese State-Driven Model**: Here, the state plays a central role, using technology for economic advancement and social control. This approach has led to significant technological development but also extensive censorship and surveillance.
- **European Rights-Driven Model**: The EU focuses on protecting individual rights, data privacy, and ensuring fair competition. Through comprehensive regulations, it seeks to balance technological innovation with societal well-being. 

*Bradford explores the "horizontal battles" among these powers as they vie to export their regulatory philosophies globally, and the "vertical battles" within their jurisdictions to control tech giants. She discusses the implications of these approaches for global digital governance and the potential emergence of a fragmented "splinternet."

books.title: Don't Believe a Word
books.summary: Don’t Believe a Word debunks common myths about language, showing that many beliefs—like the idea that modern English is declining—are timeless complaints, not evidence of decay. Shariatmadari challenges ideas such as “foreign languages have untranslatable words” and that words’ origins (etymology) determine their meaning, arguing instead that meaning comes from how words are used. He highlights the natural, evolving patterns of speech—like “aks” instead of “ask”—as valid linguistic processes, and defends nonstandard dialects like African American Vernacular English as logical and structured forms of expression. The book also questions the theories of universal grammar and the notion that language shapes thinking completely, proposing that language is something built through social use: “a road that is paved at the same time as we walk it.”

books.title: Doughnut Economics
books.summary: Doughnut Economics reimagines the purpose of economics in the 21st century by replacing the traditional focus on endless GDP growth with the goal of helping humanity thrive within a “safe and just space.” This space—the "doughnut"—is defined by two concentric boundaries: the inner social foundation, ensuring essentials like healthcare, education, equity, and political voice; and the outer ecological ceiling, guarding against planetary overshoot in areas like climate change, biodiversity loss, and land degradation. Raworth proposes seven new mindsets—from embedding the economy within society and nature, to nurturing human cooperation, embracing systems thinking, designing for distribution and regeneration, and being agnostic about growth—that guide economies toward equitable, sustainable prosperity. Her framework has inspired global experimentation, notably in cities like Amsterdam, adopting doughnut-based policies for inclusive and eco-conscious development.

books.title: Draft No. 4
books.summary: Draft No. 4 is a collection of eight insightful essays by John McPhee—drawn from The New Yorker—that serve as a master class on the craft of writing. McPhee shares his principles: begin by writing the lead to illuminate the underlying structure; build an invisible yet compelling narrative framework; embrace writing as selection, where thousands of small details coalesce into a singular impression; and understand that the real writing happens through multiple drafts—especially the fourth—when precision and clarity emerge. He encourages writing what genuinely interests you, prioritizing substance over market trends, relying on dictionaries rather than thesauruses for the right word, and confronting the insecurities that plague every writer. Through candid reflection and practical wisdom, McPhee reveals what it takes to shape nonfiction with both integrity and elegance.

books.title: Dreamers
books.summary: Dreamers profiles the aspirations and anxieties of India’s millennials from small towns and villages,a generation numbering in the hundreds of millions and more connected globally than ever yet shaped by narrow definitions of Indian identity. Through vivid case studies—from clickbait entrepreneurs and aspiring Bollywood stars, to student leaders, cow-protection vigilantes, fixers, and scam operators—Poonam reveals how these young people, desperate and ambitious, latch onto exclusionary nationalism, technology, or any route to recognition. Their hunger for respect and escape drives them—but amidst systemic failures in skills, education, and employment, their dreams may portend a turbulent future for both India and the wider world.

books.title: Dust
books.summary:
A deceptively expansive book built on a tiny thesis. Jay Owens uses airborne grit—everything from Saharan sand and volcanic ash to microplastics and nuclear fallout—as a vehicle through which he for reading the Anthropocene. The premise is immediately arresting: dust is both a legacy of industrial “progress” and an agent actively reshaping climate, health and politics.*

*Chapter by chapter, the author drags normally invisible infrastructure into view. We tour desiccated Owens Lake, now North America’s largest source of PM 10 pollution; sift Greenland snow for cosmic particles; and stand in the fallout shadow of the Nevada Test Site.* 

*In tracing a line from cosmic nebulae to the fluff beneath our beds, Dust succeeds in making the mundane sublime—and urgent. It is a persuasive argument that to confront the planet‑scale crises of the twenty‑first century, we must start with what literally hangs in the air around us. Readers of environmental non‑fiction, urban studies and travel writing alike will find Owens an engaging, unsettling guide to a world we thought we knew but, in truth, had barely seen.

books.title: Eavesdropping
books.summary: A wide-ranging exploration of the human—and animal—impulse to listen in on others. Locke traces the phenomenon from early voyeurism and communal living, where privacy was minimal, through the architectural and social changes that gave rise to hidden listening—like bell ropes and keyholes in medieval homes—to today’s digital surveillance via social media, CCTV, and phone tapping. He draws on examples from chimpanzees eavesdropping for survival cues to Parisian café gossip, from Hitchcock’s Rear Window to modern espionage, arguing that eavesdropping is rooted in biology yet shaped by cultural norms. Locke shows that while eavesdropping can serve to understand and connect, it also carries moral weight—manifesting as theft of privacy, manipulation, or control—making it a compelling lens to reflect on visibility, intimacy, and power across history and species.

books.title: Eccentric Orbits
books.summary: Eccentric Orbits tells the unlikely, behind-the-scenes story of the Iridium satellite network—conceived in the 1980s by Motorola as a revolutionary system of 66 satellites to provide global phone coverage. The project quickly spiraled into one of the most ambitious and expensive failures in business history: phones were bulky, calls were costly, and within a year of launch, Iridium was bankrupt. But through the relentless efforts of investor Dan Colussy and a small team of allies, the system was rescued from being scrapped, surviving bankruptcy court, skeptical governments, and corporate indifference to become indispensable for military operations, aviation, maritime safety, and disaster response worldwide. Bloom blends technical detail, corporate intrigue, legal battles, and personal drama into a sweeping narrative of innovation, hubris, collapse, and revival.

books.title: Edison
books.summary: Edison is a sweeping, meticulously researched biography of Thomas Alva Edison that charts the life of America’s most prolific inventor through a bold reverse-chronological structure—beginning with his final years and moving backward to his upbringing. Drawing on seven years of deep archival work, Morris portrays Edison not as a mythical genius but as an “overwhelming force of nature,” a visionary who combined compulsive creativity with relentless persistence, patented over 1,093 inventions, and founded hundreds of companies. The book dispels common myths—affirming Edison’s central role in his inventions and his talent as an entrepreneur—and explores the contradictions of his character: his near-total deafness, obsessive work ethic, brilliance alongside neglect of personal relationships, and his savvy in both invention and commercialization.

books.title: Emergence
books.summary: An accessible tour of emergence and self-organisation—the way complex, intelligent-seeming order arises from many simple parts following local rules, with no central controller. Johnson draws his examples from ant colonies, brains, cities, and software, showing how bottom-up systems learn and adapt, and how the same principles illuminate everything from urban neighbourhoods to online communities.

books.title: Empire of AI
books.summary: An investigative account of OpenAI and the wider AI industry by journalist Karen Hao, charting the company's transformation from a nonprofit research lab into a commercial powerhouse. Hao frames the pursuit of artificial general intelligence as a new kind of empire, examining the concentration of power, the hidden labour and resources behind the technology, and the human and geopolitical costs of the race to build ever-larger models.

books.title: Enemy of All Mankind
books.summary:
Enemy of All Mankind centres on the 1695 heist by pirate Henry Every, whose audacious capture of a Mughal treasure ship sparked an unprecedented global manhunt. Steven Johnson weaves this gripping narrative into a broader exploration of how this singular act helped catalyse the rise of the East India Company, the expansion of the British Empire, and the emergence of a modern global economy. The book combines sea‑shanty drama with insights into institutions—such as nascent multinational corporations and early tabloid media—and shows how a single rogue sailor’s deed rippled through geopolitics, capitalism, and culture._

***Henry Every’s audacious piracy was the pivotal inflection point that helped birth both modern global capitalism and the institutions that would shape the contemporary world.

books.title: Engineering a Nation
books.summary: Aparajith Ramnath’s biography of Sir M. Visvesvaraya doubles as a history of India’s transition from colony to modern republic: it follows the orphan from Muddenahalli through Bombay PWD apprenticeships and landmark feats such as Hyderabad’s flood-control gates and the Krishna Raja Sagara dam; shows him, as Dewan of Mysore (1912-18), parlaying engineering logic into policy—founding steel works, extending railways, reforming sanitation and education; tracks his inter-war crusade for state-led industrialisation in _Reconstructing India_ and early economic-planning debates; and ends with the centenarian advising post-1947 governments while his ideas echo in IITs and multipurpose river-valley schemes. Ramnath blends archival research, personal letters and thematic essays on water, bureaucracy and professional networks to illustrate both the promise and the limits of technocratic nation-building—all in one tightly woven narrative.

books.title: Enlightenment Now
books.summary:
Enlightenment Now defends the values of the Enlightenment—reason, science, and humanism—as the driving forces behind centuries of progress in health, prosperity, peace, safety, and human well-being. Using statistics, graphs, and global data, Pinker shows how modern life has vastly improved: people live longer, healthier, wealthier, and freer lives than ever before. Yet despite these gains, pessimism and nostalgia often obscure the reality of progress. Pinker warns that returning to tribalism, authoritarianism, magical thinking, and irrationality threatens the gains we've made and urges a renewed defence of Enlightenment ideals to sustain and build upon our advances in the world._

***Although many believe the world to be deteriorating, empirical evidence shows humanity has consistently improved and will continue to do so—if we steadfastly uphold Enlightenment principles of reason, science, and humanism.

books.title: Entangled Life
books.summary:
Entangled Life reveals the intricate and vital role fungi play in the fabric of life—beneath our feet and within our bodies. Merlin Sheldrake dives into the science and wonder of mycelial networks that connect plants through nutrient exchange, the alien biology of lichens, fungi’s influence on plant evolution, and their mind-altering power through psychedelics like psilocybin. Blending vivid storytelling with scientific rigour, he explores fungi’s contributions in fermentation, environmental cleanup, sustainable materials, and reshaping how we understand intelligence, identity, and ecological connection. The book invites readers to recognise fungi not as marginal oddities, but as central players in the ecosystems that sustain us—and as catalysts for rethinking our relationship with the living world._

***Through their vast underground networks and evolutionary partnerships, fungi fundamentally challenge human notions of individuality and intelligence, reshaping our understanding of life’s interconnectivity.

books.title: Every Living Thing
books.summary:
A historical narrative that explores the early race for classification of the natural world. It focuses on the lives and contributions of two 18th-century naturalists, Carl Linnaeus and Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon, who sought to name and categorize every living thing on Earth. This is a biography of these proto-biologists, highlighting their different backgrounds and approaches to understanding the natural world. The book progresses beyong their deaths, showing their great effect on the science.*

*Linnaeus and Buffon were rivals in the race to classify all life on Earth. Linnaeus developed a binary nomenclature and a classification system that assigned plants and animals into kingdoms, classes, orders, families, and species. Buffon, on the other hand, believed that all such systematic approaches were reductionist and flawed. Linnaeus's classification system became the standard despite its inaccuracies and racist classifications. It was easily grasped and included racist classifications of humans, which prevailed over Buffon's more nuanced understanding of nature. The legacy of Linnaeus and Buffon influenced the development of biology and evolutionary theories. Their work laid the groundwork for later scientists such as [[Lamarck]], Darwin, and Huxley, who furthered evolutionary theories and critiqued racial stereotypes.

books.title: Everybody Lies
books.summary: In **Everybody Lies**, Seth Stephens‑Davidowitz demonstrates how analysing anonymised data like Google searches and internet behaviour offers a more honest window into human nature than surveys or self-reports, where people tend to lie or present idealised versions of themselves. The book reveals unsettling truths—from widespread racism, intimate sexual fantasies, and mental health struggles to political attitudes and personal insecurities—thanks to the candid nature of anonymous search queries. Stephens‑Davidowitz also explores how childhood experiences shape lifelong preferences, the power of A/B testing, and the promise—and limits—of big data, while cautioning against ethical pitfalls and misinterpretations.

books.title: Factfulness
books.summary:
Factfulness reveals how deeply ingrained human instincts—such as our tendencies toward negativity, fear, urgency, blaming, and binary thinking—skew our understanding of the world. Rosling presents a more accurate global perspective by dividing humanity into four income-based levels instead of the outdated developing/developed dichotomy, showing that most people now live in the middle. With lively data, surprising statistics, and ten guiding instincts to recognise and counter, the book demonstrates how we systematically underestimate progress in areas like health, education, and poverty reduction. It teaches readers to think more factfully—to question sensational narratives, rely on evidence over instincts, and cultivate a worldview grounded in empirical reality._

_Our worldview is distorted by innate psychological biases that make us see the world as worse than it is. If we can train ourselves to think "factfully," using data and critical thinking, we can overturn pessimism and recognise genuine global progress.

books.title: Fancy Bear Goes Phishing
books.summary: An exploration of the history cybersecurity, focusing on the tactics and strategies employed by sophisticated cybercriminals, particularly the notorious Russian hacking group known as Fancy Bear. The book examines notable cases such as the Morris Worm of the 1980s, the exploits of the Bulgarian hacker known as "Dark Avenger," the breach of Paris Hilton's phone, the Russian cyberattacks on the Democratic National Committee, and the emergence of botnets leveraging unsecured Internet of Things devices. Through these narratives, Shapiro not only elucidates the technical methodologies employed by hackers but also provides a philosophical perspective on the motivations and societal factors contributing to these cybercrimes. Shapiro highlights the vulnerabilities in our digital lives and emphasizes the importance of cybersecurity awareness and resilience in an increasingly interconnected world.

books.title: Fantastic Numbers and Where to Find Them
books.summary: Fantastic Numbers and Where to Find Them takes readers on a tour of nine extraordinary numbers—from enormous constructs like Graham’s number and TREE(3), to incredibly small values like 10⁻¹²⁰—using each as a way to explore key ideas in quantum mechanics, cosmology, black holes, relativity, and the cosmological constant. Padilla begins with the small number 1.000000000000000858 (the time-dilation factor when Usain Bolt set his world record) to introduce relativity, then moves through “big numbers,” “little numbers,” and “infinity” to reveal how mathematics shapes our understanding of the universe. The book shows how these strange and extreme numbers illuminate fundamental mysteries of physics, the limits of proof, and the nature of reality itself.

books.title: Fire on the Ganges
books.summary:
Radhika Iyengar spent seven to eight years researching the Dom community of Varanasi. The book explores the lives of the Doms, a Dalit community that has been entrusted with the traditional role of cremating the dead at Manikarnika Ghat in Varanasi. Through interviews with members of the Dom community, Iyengar delves into their struggles, hopes, and desires, shedding light on the social fabric of the ghats and the caste system that has marginalized them.*

*The book is an exploration of the business of death in Banaras, centering the narratives of the labor that fuels the fire that is critical to the city. Iyengar's writing is empathetic and concerned, presenting the lived reality of the Doms and compelling the reader to acknowledge their plight and confront their own complicity.

books.title: Forged in Crisis
books.summary: [[Rudra Chaudhuri]]'s book on the history of Indo-US relations. A good historical perspective on the geopolitics we are now going through.

books.title: From The King's Table to Street Food
books.summary: Part culinary chronicle, part urban biography, and part family memoir, the veteran food historian sets himself a deceptively simple question—who counts as an asli Dilliwala, and what exactly is “his” cuisine?—then answers it with a 392‑page tour that begins in the Mahabharata’s Indraprastha and ends in today’s NCR food courts. Pant’s scholarship is generous, but the book’s real flavour comes from its memoiristic undertow. Drawing on seventy years of family memory—four generations who moved from Mukteshwar to the capital—he writes as both participant and historian, whether recalling childhood visits to Ghantewala for sohan halwa or jukebox afternoons at Gaylord’s after the Emergency. This personal lens keeps the sociopolitical chapters (on caste hierarchies, patriarchy and the link between cheap coffee‑house food and democratic debate) from feeling academic; the city’s food history is literally lived on the page.

books.title: Frostbite
books.summary:
Frostbite, is a bracing work of narrative science writing that asks readers to see the fridge not as a neutral kitchen appliance but as the beating (or perhaps chilling) heart of modern civilisation. Its scope is ambitious—economic history, microbiology, climate science and food anthropology intermingle—but Twilley’s brisk prose and reportorial eye keep the material as crisp as a February morning in Maine.*

*Cold, she argues, is an absence that has nonetheless reshaped everything from the height of the average American to the shape of world cities. The claim sounds hyperbolic until she piles on the evidence: lager beer fermenters that bankrolled early refrigeration, bananas whose cosmopolitan travels require “a complex blend of temperature control and atmospheric manipulation,” and orange‑juice “banks” the size of oil refineries that function as strategic reserves.

books.title: Genome
books.summary: A tour of human genetics structured as twenty-three chapters, one for each pair of human chromosomes, with each chapter using a gene on that chromosome as a window onto a larger theme. Ridley ranges across evolution, disease, intelligence, behaviour, and free will, using the newly mapped genome to tell an engaging story of what our DNA does and does not determine.

books.title: Getting Things Done
books.summary: The book that introduced the "GTD" productivity method, built on the premise that the mind is for having ideas, not holding them. Allen lays out a system for capturing every commitment into a trusted external structure, clarifying the next physical action for each, and organising and reviewing it all, so attention is freed for focused, stress-free work.

books.title: Gods, Guns and Missionaries
books.summary: Gods, Guns and Missionaries traces how modern Hindu identity emerged over centuries through encounters with colonialism, missionaries, reformers, and internal adaptation. Pillai shows that Hinduism—long a fluid, diverse tradition—was reframed under European scrutiny into a simplified, textual religion shaped by Orientalist and missionary critiques. Reformers like Raja Ram Mohan Roy and Dayananda Saraswati further "Protestantized" the tradition, elevating the Upanishads while dismissing Puranic practices. Through stories of missionaries, maharajas, Orientalists, and native reformers, the book reveals how Hinduism’s flexibility both enabled its survival and facilitated the creation of a coherent, modern identity that later fueled Hindu nationalism. Rather than portraying Hinduism as a monolith, Pillai underscores its dynamic nature and the complex historical forces that forged what we now understand as "Hindu" identity.

books.title: Governance by Stealth
books.summary:
Governance by Stealth traces how India’s Ministry of Home Affairs—the successor to the colonial Home Department—became central to the post-colonial state by wielding subtle, indirect power. Mitra explores how the institution sustained stability through minimal use of force and maximum reliance on bureaucratic expertise, negotiated order, and symbolic authority. He shows how the Ministry functioned as a bridge between political leaders and civil servants, managed challenges like princely state integration, language and religious tensions, insurgencies, and fragile nation-building. While the Ministry operated quietly and effectively for decades, its influence waned during authoritarian episodes like the Emergency, revealing the limits of stealthy governance in the absence of political legitimacy._

***India’s stability and institutional resilience emerged not from overt coercion, but from the Home Ministry’s sophisticated practice of "governance by stealth"—using minimal force, strategic regulation, and administrative ethos to build order from within.

books.title: Guardrails
books.summary: An argument that human decisions are always shaped by "guardrails"—social norms, laws, institutions, and increasingly algorithms and AI—and that the digital age calls for consciously redesigning them. Gasser and Mayer-Schönberger draw on cognitive science, economics, and public policy to make the case for guardrails that empower individual choice, account for the common good, and stay flexible as circumstances change, rather than surrendering judgment to automated systems.

books.title: Gut Feelings
books.summary:
Intuition and unconscious decision-making—far from being flawed—are often highly effective, particularly in uncertain or complex environments. Drawing on decades of research, Gigerenzer shows that we rely on simple "heuristics" or rules of thumb—such as the recognition heuristic or "Take the Best" strategy—that help us make reliable choices using limited information. These intuitive strategies often outperform detailed analyses in real-world contexts because they align with how our brains have evolved to function: quickly filtering out noise, focusing on critical cues, and adapting to environmental structure. The book challenges the conventional bias in psychology and economics that logic-based decision-making always trumps instinct, arguing instead that intelligent intuition deserves serious respect._

***In a world of uncertainty, intuition rooted in evolved, context-appropriate heuristics is superior to complex analysis. Gut feelings are the smarter side of human decision-making.

books.title: H-Pop
books.summary: H-Pop is an investigative look into the rise of "Hindutva Pop"—a subgenre of cultural content including songs, poetry, social media posts, and books—that embeds Hindu nationalist ideology into India's popular imagination. Journalist Kunal Purohit travels through small towns across India, profiling artists like rapper and poet Kavi Singh, Godse-apologist Kamal Agney, and influencer Sandeep Deo. Through their work—ranging from incendiary lyrics to historic revisionism—he shows how H-Pop normalises Islamophobia, demonises minorities, recasts historical narratives, and fuels political mobilisation without mainstream visibility. With a blend of field reporting, lyric analysis, and personal interviews, Purohit reveals how this stealthy cultural engine reinforces ideological extremism under the radar of conventional media.

books.title: Helgoland
books.summary:
Helgoland is the story of Werner Heisenberg’s breakthrough on the tiny island of Helgoland in 1925 that was the birth of quantum theory. Rovelli introduces relational quantum mechanics—the idea that physical properties do not exist in isolation but only in relation to other systems—suggesting that reality is fundamentally made of interactions rather than independent objects. He situates this view within the broader philosophical traditions of thinkers like Nagarjuna and Mach, and shows how it addresses the paradoxes and mysteries of quantum physics. By blending history, physics, and philosophy, Rovelli argues that quantum theory reshapes our understanding of knowledge, existence, and the interconnectedness of all things._

***Quantum mechanics reveals a relational universe where reality consists not of absolute entities but of networks of interactions, fundamentally altering how we conceive of existence itself.

books.title: Hello World
books.summary: Hello World explores the growing influence of algorithms and AI on everyday life, examining how they shape decisions in areas like healthcare, transportation, criminal justice, finance, and the arts. Fry argues that algorithms are not neutral—they reflect biases embedded in their data and design. Through real-world examples such as driverless cars, predictive policing, medical diagnostics, and recommendation systems, she shows both the promise and peril of algorithmic decision-making. The book highlights the moral and societal dilemmas raised by delegating judgment to machines and advocates for a “cyborg future” where humans work with, not surrender to, algorithms—retaining control, demanding transparency, and ensuring fairness.

books.title: Homo Deus
books.summary: Homo Deus explores the possible futures of humankind now that we have largely overcome famine, plague, and war—the great enemies of the past. Harari argues that the new human agenda will focus on achieving immortality, lasting happiness, and god-like powers of creation, as advances in biotechnology, artificial intelligence, and data science transform what it means to be human. He warns that the rise of “Dataism”—a worldview that prioritises information flow above individual experience—could reshape politics, economics, and morality, potentially rendering human beings less central than the algorithms they create. The book blends history, philosophy, and speculative foresight to show how our species’ pursuit of mastery may lead to radical new forms of inequality and even our obsolescence.

books.title: House of Huawei
books.summary: A deeply reported history of Huawei by Washington Post journalist Eva Dou, tracing how founder Ren Zhengfei built an obscure Shenzhen telecom firm into one of the world's most powerful technology companies. Drawing on extensive interviews and archival research, Dou examines the company's secretive culture and its entanglement with China's state and security apparatus, set against the U.S.–China trade war and the detention of Ren's daughter Meng Wanzhou.

books.title: House of the People
books.summary: An examination of India’s Lok Sabha, exploring how its composition, practices, and institutional health reflect broader democratic dynamics in a postcolonial state. Ronojoy Sen analyzes changes in parliamentarians’ demographics—age, gender, education, caste, religion, wealth, dynastic ties, and criminal background—and shows how these shifts influence policy and representation. He examines institutional challenges: the rise in parliamentary disruptions, decline in substantive deliberation, and weakening of committee functioning—especially in the context of coalition politics and deteriorating legislative quality. Sen also delves into growing concerns around corruption, criminality among lawmakers, operational breakdowns like the anti-defection law’s ineffectiveness, and the fallout of unregulated political financing.

books.title: How Innovation Works
books.summary: How Innovation Works explores how innovation is less about isolated genius and more about messy, collective progress. Ridley illustrates that innovations emerge gradually—through trial and error, serendipity, recombination, and collaboration—drawing on diverse examples from steam engines to vaccines to search engines. He emphasizes that freedom—the ability to exchange ideas, experiment, fail, and iterate—is the indispensable engine of innovation, while centralized planning, patents, and bureaucracy often hinder it. Rejecting the myth of the lone inventor, Ridley shows innovation as an evolutionary process driven by networks of people building on each other’s work, often without intending to innovate.

books.title: How Prime Ministers Decide
books.summary: How Prime Ministers Decide examines six pivotal decisions across the tenures of India’s prime ministers—from Indira Gandhi’s strategic return to power in 1980, Rajiv Gandhi’s reversal on the Shah Bano verdict, and V. P. Singh’s implementation of the Mandal Commission, to P. V. Narasimha Rao’s indecision around the Babri Masjid demolition, Atal Bihari Vajpayee’s authorization of nuclear tests, and Manmohan Singh’s pursuit of the Indo-US nuclear deal. Drawing on hundreds of interviews with prime ministers, aides, bureaucrats, policymakers, and journalists, Neerja Chowdhury provides inside perspectives on how these leaders navigated political pressures, personal convictions, and historical turning points. She reveals the human dynamics behind power, showing how decisions were shaped by context, relationships, and the interplay of ideology and pragmatism.

books.title: How the Victorians took Us to the Moon
books.summary: This is a book about the technological and scientific advancements of the Victorian era, and the innovators who laid the groundwork for modern science. It examines the era's ambitious vision, from steam power to electric innovations, and discusses the cultural and philosophical implications of these developments. Through a blend of history and futurism, Morus presents a narrative that emphasises both the achievements and the cautionary tales of 19th-century inventiveness.

books.title: How to Take Smart Notes
books.summary: How to Take Smart Notes presents the Zettelkasten method of note-taking developed by sociologist Niklas Luhmann. Ahrens explains that instead of passively collecting highlights or summaries, students and researchers should write short, permanent notes in their own words, each containing one idea, and link them to related notes in the slip-box. This network of interconnected ideas becomes a thinking partner: generating insights, revealing connections, and making the process of writing papers or books a natural outgrowth of note-making. The method emphasises three kinds of notes—fleeting notes, literature notes, and permanent notes—and integrates them into a workflow where writing and research happen simultaneously, rather than sequentially. By externalising memory and thought into a growing web of notes, the slip-box reduces cognitive overload, combats writer’s block, and turns knowledge work into a cumulative, creative process.

books.title: How to Wrap Five Eggs
books.summary: A celebrated visual study of traditional Japanese packaging, documenting how everyday goods—eggs, rice, sake, sweets, seeds—were once wrapped and bound in straw, paper, bamboo, leaves, and wood. Through photographs and commentary, Oka presents these humble, handmade containers as an expression of a design philosophy rooted in natural materials, restraint, and respect for the object being wrapped.

books.title: How to Write One Song
books.summary: A slim, encouraging guide to songwriting from Wilco frontman Jeff Tweedy, who sidesteps grand ambitions to focus on the achievable joy of writing a single song. Blending memoir with hands-on exercises for lyrics and melody, Tweedy demystifies creativity, argues that anyone can make something, and treats the daily practice of writing as its own reward.

books.title: Human Compatible
books.summary: Human Compatible challenges the prevailing model of AI that builds machines to rigidly optimize fixed human-specified goals. Russell argues that this “standard model” is inherently risky—such systems can act in ways that precisely fulfill their instructions, yet disastrously diverge from deeper human values (the “King Midas problem”). Instead, he argues that AI systems should be inherently uncertain about human preferences, learning those preferences through interaction, and remain deferential—especially by allowing themselves to be switched off. This uncertainty and deference make AI corrigible and aligned with human well-being. Russell emphasises that AI safety should start now—not after superintelligence arrives—and calls for both research into value alignment and serious governance of AI development.

books.title: I Am On The Hit List
books.summary: I Am on the Hit List investigates the assassination of Gauri Lankesh—an outspoken journalist and critic of Hindu nationalism—who was murdered outside her home in Bangalore in 2017. Through rigorous reporting, the book reconstructs her life, threats she faced, and the murky investigation that followed, revealing the ideological tensions fueling political violence in contemporary India. Romig interweaves Lankesh’s personal story with broader themes of rising authoritarianism, diminishing press freedom, and the fragility of democracy, while vividly portraying Bangalore’s cultural contradictions—from its literary bookstores to its tech-fueled wealth and ideological clashes. The result is both a gripping true-crime narrative and a sobering commentary on India’s slide toward intolerance.

books.title: I Contain Multitudes
books.summary: Microbes are not mere germs, they are our fundamental partners in the story of life. These microscopic organisms outnumber our own cells, shape our immune systems, influence brain development, defend animals from predators, and have constructed ecosystems—from glowing squid to coral reefs. More than half our bodies are microbial, and their interdependence with hosts is vital to how animals grow, communicate, and survive. Modern human habits—overuse of antibiotics, excessive sanitation, and habitat disruption—can unbalance these microbial ecosystems, with consequences for everything from allergies to reef collapse.

books.title: ISRO - A Personal History
books.summary: A firsthand memoir by R. Aravamudan, one of the early pioneers of India’s space program, co-written with his wife Gita. The book traces his 50-year journey starting in 1962—from the formation of INCOSPAR under Dr. Vikram Sarabhai, through the establishment of the Thumba Equatorial Rocket Launching Station, and his training at NASA, to key milestones such as the launch of Aryabhata, the development of SLV, PSLV, GSLV, and the advancement of satellite capabilities. Aravamudan shares vivid anecdotes: engineers working in a converted church in humble Thumba, navigating international embargoes, and the evolution of the distinctly Indian institutional culture that came to be known as the “ISRO Way.” Far from a technical manual, the memoir offers an evocative insider’s perspective on how a fledgling organisation overcame resource constraints to become a leading space power.

books.title: Iconoclast
books.summary: Iconoclast is a deeply researched, critically reflective biography of B. R. Ambedkar that strips away reverential myth to reveal the full complexity of the man. Teltumbde uses archival materials and photographs to trace Ambedkar through seven life phases—from his childhood and education to his constitutional role and eventual embrace of Buddhism—and then examines how his legacy has been iconized. Rather than offering a hagiography, Teltumbde highlights Ambedkar’s contradictions: his limited class-based mobilisation, antipathy toward communism, inconsistencies in political stances, and the ways in which Ambedkarism has been co-opted and depoliticised. The author calls for a renewed, critical engagement with Ambedkar’s ideas—seeing him not as a demi-god but as an inspiring human whose vision must be engaged with honestly if a meaningful, post-Ambedkar democratic movement is to emerge.

books.title: If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies
books.summary: A stark warning from AI-safety researchers Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares that building superhuman artificial intelligence with current techniques would, on their analysis, almost certainly lead to human extinction. They argue that such a system's goals could not be reliably aligned with ours and that a single failure would be unrecoverable, calling for a halt to the race toward superintelligence before it is too late.

books.title: If Then
books.summary: If Then uncovers the forgotten story of the Simulmatics Corporation, a Cold War-era venture that pioneered data-driven prediction by creating a “People Machine” aimed at forecasting human behavior—from voting and consumer habits to civil unrest. Founded in 1959, Simulmatics blended computer simulation with behavioral science to influence politics, advertising, and counterinsurgency. Despite early successes, including claims of aiding Kennedy’s 1960 campaign, the company collapsed amid failed military contracts and ethical controversies. Lepore’s meticulously researched narrative shows how Simulmatics anticipated the future of algorithmic manipulation, linking a short-lived 1960s enterprise to the foundations of today’s predictive technology giants and their societal impact.

books.title: In Service of the Republic
books.summary:
