A masterful exploration of the complexities and challenges of designing and implementing effective public policy in India. Drawing on their extensive experience as policymakers and economists, the authors provide a deep, analytical framework for understanding the interplay between economics, politics, and governance in crafting policies that serve the public good.*

*The book is a primer on the principles of public policy, emphasizing the importance of aligning policy objectives with societal goals. Kelkar and Shah argue that good policymaking must balance competing interests, mitigate unintended consequences, and remain adaptable to the evolving needs of citizens. They stress the role of evidence-based decision-making, transparency, and accountability as essential pillars of sound governance.*

*This is literally **the** textbook for aspiring policymakers, offering actionable insights into the art and science of crafting effective public policy. With its clear-eyed analysis and deep commitment to democratic values, the book serves as a call to action for those seeking to address India’s pressing challenges through thoughtful, inclusive, and evidence-driven policymaking.

books.title: India After Gandhi
books.summary: This is the seminal work on modern India and the reason why the NIF exists. Once you read this you can understand why Ram wanted to set up the Fellowship and you can literally see all the books of scholarship that were seeded by the brief mentions in this book.

books.title: India Connected
books.summary: India Connected explores how the smartphone has rapidly become the most powerful tool in shaping modern Indian life—impacting everything from education and entrepreneurship to politics and social norms. Journalist Ravi Agrawal divides his analysis into three parts—Opportunity, Society, and the State—using vivid stories such as a rural woman teaching internet literacy, a young man mastering spoken English via apps, and the evolution of digital payments like PayTM accelerated by demonetization. He also addresses darker shifts: the spread of fake news on WhatsApp, mental health effects of smartphone addiction, challenges to net neutrality, and state surveillance in regions such as Kashmir. Agrawal presents the smartphone as both a catalyst for aspiration and progress, and a vehicle for inequality, misinformation, and political control.

books.title: India's Forgotten Country
books.summary: India’s Forgotten Country brings together over three decades of Bela Bhatia’s fieldwork, blending personal narrative and journalistic rigor to illuminate the lives of India’s most marginalized—Adivasis, Dalits, bonded laborers, tribal women, and conflict-affected communities across regions like Chhattisgarh’s Bastar, Central Bihar, Rajasthan, Telangana, Nagaland, Kashmir, and more. Bhatia combines historical context—highlighting colonial-era dispossession, forest laws, land alienation—with on-the-ground reporting that highlights state violence, displacement, resource extraction, Maoist conflict, and erasure of democratic rights. Her chapters center vivid individual testimonies—from voices like Deepa Musahar and Zarifa Begum—transforming statistics into stories of resilience, resistance, and survival. The book offers a powerful challenge to mainstream narratives by shifting attention from urban success to rural struggle, refusing pity while honoring courage, and urging readers to rethink development through the lens of the marginal, not the metropolis.

books.title: India's Near East
books.summary: India’s Near East frames India’s eastern frontier—including its northeastern states alongside Bangladesh and Myanmar—as a single [[geopolitical]] region shaped by a complex history of partition, insurgency, and state-building. Paliwal argues that India's “Act East” policy masks a deeper priority: political stability over economic opportunity. He shows how New Delhi has long balanced domestic concerns in the northeast with foreign relations involving Dhaka and Yangon—from early support for military regimes in Burma and intervention in Bangladesh, to managing secessionist movements, Mastering security strategies amid a “two-and-a-half front” threat, and later shifting toward connectivity. Across three eras—Solidarity (1947–70), Security (1971–90), and Connectivity (1991–2024)—the book traces India’s faltering attempts to assert control and foster integration in a region rich in potential yet deeply divided by history.

books.title: Indica
books.summary: Indica traces the geological and biological evolution of the Indian subcontinent over billions of years, from the ancient rocks beneath cities like Ellora to the real-life dinosaurs—such as Rajasaurus—and fossils like crocodile eggs in Mumbai. Pranay Lal weaves together vivid, McPhee-style narratives drawn from extensive research, field travel, and interviews with scientists, bringing to life deserts that once hosted jellyfish, glaciated plateaus, tectonic shifts, and ecosystems rich in prehistoric creatures. Along the way, he explains plate tectonics, paleoenvironmental changes, hominid migration, and the erosion of geological heritage amid urban expansion and mining. The book blends science, storytelling, and conservation advocacy, inviting readers to see the everyday landscape as a living archive of Earth’s deep past.

books.title: Indira Gandhi and the Years That Transformed India
books.summary: Srinath's masterful biography of Indira Gandhi with a whole host of new material from the archives. But he did not speak to Sonia for this.

books.title: Inglorious Empire
books.summary: Inglorious Empire offers a forceful and richly detailed rebuttal of colonial justifications, exposing how British rule systematically deindustrialized, impoverished, and fragmented India for its own gain. Tharoor traces the decline of India's share in global GDP from around 23% in 1700 to about 3–4% by independence, argues that British-introduced railways, laws, and education served empire—not Indians—and highlights policies like “divide and rule” and engineered famines that inflicted lasting social and economic damage. He dismantles the notion of “enlightened despotism,” framing colonialism as extraction disguised as development, and contends that any perceived benefits were incidental and largely served British strategic and economic interests.

books.title: Internet Daemons
books.summary: A study of the little-known background programs—"daemons"—that quietly run the internet's infrastructure, managing and prioritising the flow of data packets. Media scholar Fenwick McKelvey traces their lineage from the Victorian thought experiment of Maxwell's Demon to today's networks, and shows, through cases like network-neutrality fights and traffic throttling, how much control over communication has been ceded to these automated, largely invisible agents.

books.title: Invisible Empire
books.summary: Invisible Empire presents viruses not as mere pathogens but as a vast, dynamic empire—diverse, complex, and essential to life. Pranay Lal journeys through their evolutionary origins, ecological functions, and cultural significance, unspooling stories that range from the invisible forces shaping human biology to their roles in global change: how viral remnants in our genome enabled mammalian pregnancy, how viruses sculpt ecosystems, the historical impacts of pandemics, and even the role of viruses in tulip mania and zombie-like behavior in animals. With vivid storytelling, rich illustrations, and interdisciplinary curiosity, Lal invites readers to see viruses with both awe and understanding—as integral, ambivalent, and profoundly influential players in the natural world.

books.title: Invisible Women
books.summary: Invisible Women reveals how a pervasive gender data gap—where male norms are treated as the default—pervades everything from healthcare and workplace design to urban planning, technology, and policy. Drawing on global case studies, Pérez shows how women are systematically excluded: from crash-test dummies designed only for the “average male,” to misdiagnoses due to male-centric medical research, to smartphones sized for male hands and inadequate snow-clearing patterns that ignore women’s daily travel routes. The book is a vivid chronicle of how major systems continue to overlook—or misrepresent—the needs of half the human population, resulting in inefficiencies, risks, and injustices.

books.title: Iru - The Remarkable Life of Irawati Karve
books.summary: Iru is the biography of Irawati “Iru” Karve—India’s pioneering female anthropologist. The authors trace her early education in Burma and Pune, her daring journey to earn a PhD in anthropology in 1920s Berlin under Eugen Fischer (and how she challenged his race-based theories), and her later career leading anthropology in India. Intertwined are vivid portraits of her progressive marriage, life-long curiosity, empathetic field research across rural India, and her profound reflections on kinship, caste, mythology, and modernity. Through intimate detail—a whisper of apology to measured skulls in Berlin, scooting through Pune on her Lambretta, and exploring folklore as much as science—the book brings alive Iru’s intellect, independence, contradictions, and quiet courage.

books.title: Jacquard's Web
books.summary: Jacquard’s Web traces the surprising technological lineage from a 19th-century silk-weaving loom in Napoleonic France to the computers we use today. James Essinger vividly recounts how Joseph-Marie Jacquard’s invention of the programmable loom—using punched cards to control weaving patterns—dramatically increased productivity and functioned as the precursor to computer programming. The book links this innovation through figures like Charles Babbage, who borrowed the idea for his Analytical Engine, Ada Lovelace, who recognized its programming potential, Herman Hollerith, who applied punched cards to census tabulation, and IBM’s evolution under Thomas Watson and Howard Aiken’s early computerized machines. Essinger weaves together engineering ingenuity, business history, and cultural change, showing how a device designed for decorative cloth patterns ultimately spun the threads of modern computing.

books.title: Kashmir Under 370
books.summary:
A memoir of Mahendra Sabharwal, the first Indian Police Service (IPS) officer directly assigned to the Jammu and Kashmir cadre in 1964 who served the state for nearly four decades, culminating his career as the Director General of Police. The book provides an analytical personal history of Jammu and Kashmir, reflecting on the years and lives lost, and critiquing the political maneuvers that have hindered the state's progress. Through Sabharwal's eyes, readers gain insights into the prime ministers, governors, chief ministers, and politicians who have influenced Kashmir's destiny. His firsthand accounts offer an unfiltered view of the challenges faced during pivotal events, such as managing the aftermath of Zulfikar Bhutto's execution, handling the sieges of Hazratbal, and overseeing the funeral processions of separatist leaders. 

A significant portion of the memoir addresses the abrogation of Article 370, which granted special autonomy to Jammu and Kashmir. Sabharwal contends that the removal of this article, along with India's economic growth and assertive responses to cross-border terrorism, has set the stage for a more hopeful future for the region. He acknowledges that while these developments are promising, substantial work remains to achieve lasting peace and stability.

books.title: Land of Seven Rivers
books.summary: An engaging journey through India’s history—woven through its landscape—from geological formation and tectonic shifts that shaped the Himalayas to the cultural, economic, and civilizational ebbs and flows along its major rivers like the Indus, Ganges, and the (now fossil) Saraswati. Sanjeev Sanyal blends geology, archaeology, mythology, and environmental change to show how river systems directed settlement, trade routes, mythology, and urban growth. He traces ancient trade through Southeast Asia, the persistence of historical transport corridors in modern highways, and interprets regional shifts—from an open, entrepreneurial culture to periods of introspection. Throughout, he encourages readers to see India’s present through the lens of its deeply layered physical and human geography.

books.title: Leonardo da Vinci - The Biography
books.summary: A richly illustrated life of the Renaissance polymath, drawn largely from Leonardo's own thousands of pages of notebooks. Isaacson presents him as the supreme example of curiosity for its own sake—a restless, often distracted genius whose art and science fed each other—tracing how his obsessive observation of anatomy, water, light, and flight informed masterpieces like the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, and arguing that his creativity sprang from standing at the intersection of the humanities and the sciences.

books.title: Life Among the Scorpions
books.summary: Jaya Jaitly’s candid political memoir spanning thirty tumultuous years in Indian politics. She traces her roots to a matrilineal royal family in Kerala and recounts an international childhood, the loss of her father, education abroad, and a return to India where she became deeply involved in crafts advocacy—including founding Dilli Haat and the Dastkari Haat Samiti—to uplift artisans. Her political journey under firebrand George Fernandes brought her into national prominence as Samata Party president and into controversies such as the Tehelka sting. Through personal and political upheaval—handling allegations, fighting for artisans, navigating alliances, and confronting betrayal—Jaitly portrays Indian politics as a dangerous arena for women, where trust is scarce and survival requires resilience.

books.title: Life on the Edge
books.summary: "Life on the Edge"  argues that the seemingly miraculous properties of life itself may be explained through quantum mechanics operating at a biological level. The authors contend that quantum effects, previously thought to occur only in the subatomic realm, play a crucial role in fundamental biological processes like [[photosynthesis]], animal navigation, and even our sense of smell. Through detailed examination of scientific research and accessible explanations of complex concepts, they demonstrate how [[quantum tunelling]], [[superposition]], and [[entanglement]] might be essential to life's basic functions, rather than being limited to the quantum physics laboratory. It argues that the boundary between the quantum and biological worlds is far more blurred than previously thought, and that [[quantum mechanics]] may be the missing piece in our understanding of how life originated and continues to function with such remarkable efficiency and precision.

books.title: Made in India
books.summary: The intertwined story of the Indian pharmaceutical industry, the company Lupin, and its founder Desh Bandhu Gupta—a village boy from Rajasthan who became a teacher and professor before building a generics firm worth billions. Written candidly by entrepreneur Manish Sabharwal and journalist Sundeep Khanna, it is a portrait of institution-building without mythmaking, confronting the crises, failures, and personal costs alongside the achievements.

books.title: Managing the Professional Service Firm
books.summary: Maister collates decades of insights into how professional services firms differ from other types of businesses—how strategy, people, culture, partner/leadership structure, client relationships, leverage (ratio of senior to junior staff), profitability, marketing, and motivation all need to be managed together. He draws out both theoretical frameworks (like stages in a professional‐firm lifecycle) and very practical rules (how to delegate, how to hire, how to reward, how to govern partnerships) so that firms can grow without losing quality or creating internal dysfunction.

books.title: Matchmakers
books.summary: Matchmakers explains how modern businesses like Uber, Airbnb, Alibaba, and OpenTable operate as **multisided platforms**, or “matchmakers,” by connecting different groups—such as riders and drivers, hosts and guests, buyers and sellers—through a shared digital or physical venue. The authors analyze the **distinctive economics** of these platforms, showing how they must attract a critical mass on both sides to function (solving the “chicken-and-egg” problem), determine pricing by often subsidising one side while charging the other, and continuously reduce **transactional friction** to create value. They explore strategic approaches—like zig-zag or two-step tactics—to achieve ignition and contend with network effects, governance, ecosystem complexity, and trust. Through historical and contemporary examples (OpenTable, YouTube, M-PESA, e-commerce malls), the book demonstrates how a platform’s design—its pricing, depth, regulation, and experience—makes or breaks its success.

books.title: Mathematica
books.summary: A mathematician's argument that mathematics is not really about logic or formal proof but about cultivating intuition—a physical, almost meditative practice of learning to "see" abstract things, closer to yoga than to problem sets. Bessis dismantles the myth of innate genius, links mathematical understanding to ordinary milestones like learning to walk and speak, and offers sensory exercises meant to show that this hidden inner faculty is available to anyone. This book is a refreshing demystification of how mathematical discoveries come to be that makes the entire process more accessible to the lay person.

books.title: Midnight's Borders
books.summary: Midnight’s Borders is a profound work of narrative reportage in which Suchitra Vijayan undertakes a seven-year, 9,000-mile journey tracing India’s contested borders—from Afghanistan and Pakistan to Bangladesh, Myanmar, and China. Through vivid, empathetic storytelling—mixed with photographs, personal testimonies, archival material, and poetry—she chronicles the human cost of borders arbitrarily drawn and fiercely enforced. Villages split, families rendered stateless, homes swallowed by shifting rivers in the Sundarbans, and trauma inflicted by floodlights or militarisation all emerge as haunting realities. Vijayan spotlights peoples’ lives disrupted by colonial cartography, nationalist citizenship tests, and present-day policies, revealing a hidden India that rarely makes headlines. She centres her narrative not on state power, but on the lived experiences of those for whom borders are unending scars—stories of survival, erasure, and resilience at the edges of the map.

books.title: Mine!
books.summary: Mine! explores how ownership is shaped not by timeless natural truths, but by socially constructed stories and rules—a toolkit of narratives we use to claim what’s ours. Heller and Salzman identify six core “ownership stories”—like “first come, first served,” “possession is nine-tenths of the law,” “you reap what you sow,” “my home is my castle,” “our bodies, ourselves,” and “the meek shall inherit the earth.” These maxims serve as competing rationales used to assert claims over resources, possessions, and ideas. The authors illustrate how these narratives influence everything from everyday conflicts—like reclaiming space behind a reclining airplane seat—to critical issues, such as how tangled patent rights can hinder medical innovation. Through legal metaphors like the “bundle of sticks,” the book examines how ownership is constructed, contested, and deployed—and how the rules we choose shape access, equity, and creativity in society.

books.title: More From Less
books.summary: In More from Less, Andrew McAfee presents a compelling and data-rich story of how rich, technological economies—especially the U.S.—have begun improving human prosperity while reducing their environmental footprint. Contrary to the long-held belief that growth always comes at nature’s expense, resource consumption (metals, energy, timber, cropland, pollution) has decreased even as population and GDP have climbed. McAfee attributes this unprecedented shift to the combined forces of capitalism (which seeks cost reductions) and technological innovation (especially digital tools that substitute atoms with bits), supported by rising public awareness and responsive governance—the “four horsemen of the optimist”. He emphasizes that this shift didn’t rely on radical societal upheaval, but rather on accelerating the efficiencies already enabled by free markets and modern technology. While acknowledging remaining challenges—such as climate change and inequality—McAfee’s message is that progress toward a greener, more abundant future is already underway and can be accelerated.

books.title: Most Delicious Poison
books.summary: Explores how humanity’s long relationship with natural toxins has shaped our biology, culture, and evolution. Drawing from biochemistry, evolutionary biology, and history, Whiteman shows how plants and animals evolved chemical defenses that humans learned to exploit—transforming poisons into medicines, stimulants, and pleasures. From caffeine, nicotine, and capsaicin to opiates, cocaine, and snake venom, he traces how these molecules interact with our nervous systems and how our genes have adapted to tolerate, crave, or depend on them. The book reveals that what we call “poison” is often a matter of dose and context, and that the same compounds that can kill us have driven creativity, trade, and scientific discovery. It ends by suggesting that our relationship with toxins mirrors our broader engagement with nature—simultaneously perilous and indispensable.

books.title: Mother Mary Comes to Me
books.summary: A memoir centered on Roy's fierce, charismatic, and domineering mother, Mary Roy—the Kerala educator and activist who founded a school and won a landmark Supreme Court case securing Syrian Christian women equal inheritance rights. Roy traces her flight from her mother at eighteen, their lifelong entanglement of love and resentment, and how that combustible relationship shaped her into a writer her mother both made possible and begrudged.

books.title: My Life as a Quant
books.summary: A memoir of Derman's passage from theoretical particle physics to the heart of Wall Street, where he became one of the pioneering "quants" at Goldman Sachs. He reflects on the culture clash between academic physics and finance, the seductions and limits of mathematical modeling of markets, and what is lost and gained when a physicist turns his tools on money rather than nature.

books.title: Nano Comes to Life
books.summary: Nano Comes to Life explores the groundbreaking intersection of nanotechnology and biology, revealing how manipulating matter at the nanoscale—right down to proteins and DNA—is transforming our understanding of life. Sonia Contera, a biological physicist, describes how tools like atomic force microscopy allow us to see and interact with biomolecules, enabling applications such as DNA origami, nanoscale machines that target cancer cells, nano-antibiotics against resistant bacteria, and engineered tissues and organs. The book presents nanotechnology as a multidisciplinary fusion of physics, biology, engineering, robotics, and AI. Contera describes its revolutionary potential for human health and longevity, while also inviting us to reflect on its ethical dimensions and shared benefits within this emerging "transmaterial era"

books.title: New Dark Age
books.summary: In New Dark Age, James Bridle explores how the overwhelming deluge of data and our uncritical faith in computing is not clarifying the world—but making it harder to understand. He argues that the Enlightenment belief that more information equates to better understanding has collapsed in the face of digital overload, computational arrogance, and algorithmic opacity. Bridle traces how reliance on data-driven models and automation fosters “automation bias," eroding our ability to think critically and detect truth behind digital signals. He extends the metaphor of the “cloud” to describe how tech obscures more than it reveals, shrouding infrastructure, power, and intent beneath layers of systems we neither see nor understand. Far from heralding a new Enlightenment, our age may instead be ushering in a "new Dark Age"—an era of catastrophic uncertainty, fractured consensus, and diminishing comprehension. Bridle doesn’t call for disconnection but for "systemic literacy": a cultural shift to understanding how digital systems work and embracing uncertainty amid unseen complexity.

books.title: Nexus
books.summary: In Nexus, Harari surveys the long arc of information networks—tracing their power from prehistoric storytelling and sacred texts to the printing press, mass media, bureaucracies, and the digital era culminating in artificial intelligence. He argues that the ability to share and shape information has always been central to social cohesion and political control—and that each breakthrough has unleashed both unity and instability. While these networks have advanced human cooperation and knowledge, they’ve also enabled manipulation, myth-making, and mass delusion—from witch hunts and totalitarian propaganda to today’s algorithmic echo chambers. As AI becomes an “alien intelligence” that can weave narratives and shape reality beyond human comprehension, Harari issues a stark warning: the tools that once helped societies thrive may now threaten democracy, truth, and human agency.

books.title: Nudge
books.summary: Nudge introduces the concept of **“libertarian paternalism”**—the idea that governments and organizations can structure choices in ways that guide people toward better decisions while preserving individual freedom. Thaler and Sunstein explain that humans are prone to cognitive biases and heuristics (like loss aversion, status quo bias, and anchoring) that often lead to poor outcomes in areas such as saving for retirement, choosing healthcare, or adopting healthy habits. By designing choice architectures—such as setting beneficial defaults (automatic enrollment in pensions), framing options differently, or simplifying complex decisions—institutions can “nudge” people toward choices that improve their welfare without restricting alternatives. The book argues that nudges are a practical, low-cost way to address widespread policy and personal challenges, balancing freedom of choice with behavioral insights.

books.title: Nuts and Bolts
books.summary: Nuts and Bolts is a book by Roma Agarwal about 7 small inventions that changed the world.

books.title: Of Law and Life - Upendra Baxi
books.summary: A book-length conversation with the eminent Indian legal scholar Upendra Baxi, drawn from recordings made in Bangalore with a group of his former students. Across the exchanges Baxi offers a sweeping personal account of his six decades of engagement with modern Indian history, jurisprudence, and human rights, illuminating both the man and the intellectual tradition of critical, socially engaged legal scholarship he helped shape.

books.title: On Writing Well
books.summary: A comprehensive manual on how to write clear, concise, and engaging prose across all forms of nonfiction. Zinsser emphasises simplicity, economy, and humanity in writing—urging writers to strip away clutter, avoid jargon, and find their authentic voice. He covers principles of good writing such as clarity, tone, and structure, as well as practical guidance for specific genres like interviews, travel writing, memoir, and business writing. Through examples and reflections drawn from decades of teaching and editing, Zinsser shows that writing is a process of thinking clearly and rewriting relentlessly. The book concludes that good writing is fundamentally an expression of respect—for language, for the reader, and for one’s own ideas—and that mastery comes through constant refinement and honesty.

books.title: Once Upon a Prime
books.summary: In “Once Upon a Prime,” Sarah Hart argues that mathematics and literature are deeply intertwined. She explores how mathematical ideas—like geometry in Moby-Dick, statistical thinking in George Eliot, fractal structures in Jurassic Park, and geometric puzzles in Alice in Wonderland—permeate works from poets to novelists. Hart examines structural patterns in rhyme, meter, and form, highlights experimental literature like Oulipo’s constraints and Queneau’s combinatorial sonnets, and profiles authors who integrate math either explicitly or as thematic underpinnings. She demonstrates that recognising these links enriches both the reading of literature and the appreciation of mathematics.

books.title: Origin Story
books.summary: Origin Story presents the “Big History” of the universe, weaving together insights from cosmology, geology, biology, anthropology, and history into a single, coherent narrative. David Christian organizes this account around a series of “thresholds”—moments when increasing complexity gave rise to new forms of order: the Big Bang, the formation of stars and galaxies, the creation of Earth and the emergence of life, the evolution of humans with language and collective learning, the agricultural revolution, and the modern era shaped by fossil fuels and global networks. He emphasises energy flows and the Goldilocks principle (conditions being “just right”) as the drivers of complexity, culminating in today’s Anthropocene epoch, where humans wield planetary-scale influence. The book situates human history in a cosmic framework, highlighting both our fragility and responsibility in shaping the future.

books.title: Our Biggest Experiment
books.summary: Alice Bell’s _Our Biggest Experiment: An Epic History of the Climate Crisis_ takes a long view of global warming, stretching the story back three centuries to trace how coal‑fired curiosity evolved into an inadvertent planetary experiment. A former science journalist and campaigner, Bell balances panoramic sweep with character‑driven vignettes—from Eunice Foote’s forgotten 1856 greenhouse‑gas demo to Svante Arrhenius’s chilly Stockholm calculations and the tree‑hugging Bishnoi women of Rajasthan—making the book feel equal parts adventure saga and cautionary tale.

books.title: Playing to the Edge
books.summary: Playing to the Edge is Michael Hayden’s memoir of his years leading the National Security Agency (1999–2005) and the CIA (2006–2009) during the most turbulent phase of the post-9/11 era. Hayden recounts how intelligence agencies expanded surveillance, interrogation, and covert operations to confront terrorism, cyber threats, and emerging global rivals, often under intense political and legal scrutiny. He defends programs such as warrantless wiretapping and enhanced surveillance, arguing they were lawful responses to unprecedented threats, while also acknowledging public mistrust and the frictions with Congress, the courts, and civil liberties advocates. The book provides insider perspectives on operations in Iraq and Afghanistan, debates on drones, relations with the Bush and Obama administrations, and the challenges of transforming secretive agencies in a digital, hyper-connected world.

books.title: Possible Minds
books.summary:
Possible Minds is a thought-provoking collection of essays from twenty-five leading thinkers, curated by John Brockman, that explores the future of **artificial intelligence (AI)** and its profound implications for humanity. Inspired by Norbert Wiener’s 1950 book The Human Use of Human Beings, this anthology examines the promises, challenges, and existential risks of AI as it evolves from a tool to a transformative force in society._

_The essays delve into critical questions about AI ethics, governance, and the societal impact of automation. Will AI systems amplify inequality? Could they become autonomous agents with unintended consequences? How can we ensure that the development of AI aligns with humanity’s broader interests? The authors grapple with these issues, offering both optimism and caution._

_This is both a celebration of human ingenuity and a sober reminder of the responsibilities that come with developing powerful technologies. It serves as a guide to navigating the complex, rapidly changing landscape of AI and is essential reading for anyone seeking to understand the profound ways in which AI will shape the future of humanity.

books.title: Power and Progress
books.summary: A thousand-year history of technology arguing that innovation does not automatically bring shared prosperity—who benefits depends on how power is distributed and what choices societies make. The economists show how gains from major advances, from the agricultural revolution to industrialization, were often captured by narrow elites until countervailing forces redirected them, and they apply this lesson to artificial intelligence, warning it may concentrate wealth and surveillance unless deliberately steered otherwise.

books.title: Prediction Machines
books.summary: Prediction Machines centers on the idea that the recent AI revolution is less about replicating human intelligence and more about making prediction extremely cheap, accurate, and scalable. Prediction—filling in missing information using data—is a core but often invisible component of intelligence. As prediction becomes less costly, it reshapes decision-making processes, business models, and human roles. While machine prediction improves, the value of human judgment, data acquisition, and decision execution—the complements to prediction—increases at an even faster rate.

books.title: Quanta and Fields
books.summary: The second volume of Carroll's "Biggest Ideas in the Universe" series, a lucid introduction to quantum field theory for readers willing to engage with real equations. Carroll builds up from quantum mechanics to fields, particles, and the Standard Model, aiming to convey not just analogies but the actual mathematical machinery physicists use to describe reality at its most fundamental level.

books.title: Quantum Supremacy
books.summary: Quantum Supremacy presents quantum computing as humanity's next great technological leap, explaining how quantum mechanics—especially phenomena like superposition and entanglement—enable vastly more powerful computation than traditional silicon-based systems. Kaku outlines the evolution of computing from Turing machines and transistors to quantum bits (qubits), profiles the cutting-edge research being pursued by governments and tech companies, and explores the wide-ranging implications for solving major global challenges such as disease, climate change, food scarcity, and sustainable energy. However, he cautions that quantum computing remains in its infancy, with significant practical hurdles still to overcome. The narrative is speculative and visionary, highlighting quantum computing’s potential to revolutionise everything, while also acknowledging that much of this future remains uncertain and speculative.

books.title: Range
books.summary: Range challenges the belief that early specialisation is the surest path to success, arguing instead that in complex, unpredictable environments, generalists—those who explore widely, sample different domains, and connect ideas across fields—are more likely to excel. David Epstein contrasts the “Tiger Woods model” of early, focused training with the “Roger Federer model” of late specialisation after broad exploration, showing that the latter often produces more adaptable and creative problem-solvers. Drawing on case studies from sports, science, technology, and business, he demonstrates that generalists thrive because they can transfer knowledge, spot analogies, and innovate in ways that narrow experts often cannot. He stresses that while specialisation works in “kind” environments with stable rules and feedback (like chess or golf), most of the modern world is a “wicked” environment, where flexibility and broad thinking matter most.

books.title: Read Write Own
books.summary: Read Write Own outlines a bold, three-era vision of the internet’s evolution: the **“Read” era**, where the web democratized access to information; the **“Read–Write” era**, dominated by corporate platforms like Facebook and Twitter, which centralized publishing and captured most of the value; and the emerging **“Read–Write–Own” era**, powered by blockchain networks that enable users not only to create content but to **own, govern, and profit from the digital networks they help build**. Dixon argues that blockchain is not a speculative technology, but a **new foundational architecture** that can **redistribute ownership and power**—reversing centralization and restoring the internet’s dynamic, creative spirit. He distinguishes between “computer culture” (long-term builders) and “casino culture” (short-term speculators), arguing the former must guide this transformation. The book covers internet history, network economics, token design, community governance, and the potential of decentralized networks to reinvigorate innovation and civic digital life.

books.title: Replaceable You
books.summary: Roach's characteristically curious and irreverent tour of the science of replacing worn-out or missing body parts, from artificial organs and prosthetic limbs to transplants and regenerative medicine. She reports from operating rooms and labs around the world—pig-organ farms in China, cataract surgeries in Mongolia, a penis-prosthetic clinic in Georgia, an iron lung she climbs into herself—turning the messy, ingenious business of engineering the human body into wry, humane popular science.

books.title: Rise of the Robots
books.summary: Rise of the Robots examines how accelerating advances in automation, artificial intelligence, and robotics are transforming the global economy and threatening large-scale technological unemployment. Ford argues that unlike past industrial revolutions, the current wave of automation is eroding jobs across both blue- and white-collar sectors, as machines and algorithms increasingly perform not just routine labor but cognitive and creative tasks once thought uniquely human. He traces the implications for productivity, inequality, and social stability, showing how automation could hollow out the middle class and concentrate wealth in the hands of capital owners. The book concludes by calling for systemic responses—such as universal basic income, new models of education, and policies that redistribute productivity gains—to sustain economic demand and preserve social cohesion in an era of machine dominance.

books.title: Rule Makers, Rule Breakers
books.summary: Rule Makers, Rule Breakers examines how the strength of social norms—whether cultures are “tight” (strict, rule-bound, emphasizing order and conformity) or “loose” (flexible, permissive, valuing individual freedom)—shapes behavior, politics, business, and conflict around the world. Michele Gelfand draws on cross-cultural psychology and global research to show how historical threats like famine, warfare, or natural disasters push societies to adopt tighter norms, while safer, more stable contexts foster looser ones. She illustrates how this tight–loose spectrum explains national differences (Japan vs. Brazil), organizational cultures, family dynamics, and even U.S. political divides. The book also highlights the strengths and weaknesses of each orientation—tight cultures can foster order but risk rigidity, while loose cultures encourage creativity but risk chaos—and argues that success often depends on striking the right balance between the two.

books.title: Rules for a Flat World
books.summary: Rules for a Flat World explains how legal systems evolved to enable large-scale cooperation and commerce, and why today’s laws and institutions are failing to keep up with globalisation, digital platforms, and rapid innovation. Gillian Hadfield argues that law is not just a set of commands from governments but a critical infrastructure—like roads or the internet—that allows strangers to trust one another, transact, and build prosperity. She traces the history of how rules, courts, and enforcement mechanisms allowed societies to scale beyond small communities, and shows how current systems—slow, costly, and dominated by professional lawyers—are mismatched to the needs of a fast, interconnected global economy. Hadfield calls for reinventing legal infrastructure: opening it up to new providers, technologies, and business models, and treating law as a dynamic, competitive service that fosters trust, fairness, and growth.

books.title: Rules
books.summary: In Rules, historian Lorraine Daston explores the evolution of rules throughout Western history, drawing on examples ranging from cookbooks and monastic guidelines to traffic laws and algorithms. She identifies three enduring forms of rules—models (paradigms to follow), laws (normative directives), and algorithms (fixed, mechanical instructions)—and introduces the distinction between **“thick rules”**, which are flexible and nuanced, and **“thin rules”**, which are rigid and context-free. Daston traces how societies have moved between these forms, showing how thick rules remain necessary when real-world variability demands discretion, while thin rules prevail in standardised systems. She examines how algorithmic thinking reshapes our use of rules and highlights the tensions created when exceptions and human judgment collide with inflexible regulations. Throughout, she demonstrates that rules are not merely constraints, but culturally shaped tools reflecting how we balance order, interpretation, and human complexity.

books.title: Sandworm
books.summary: Sandworm investigates the shadowy Russian cyberwarfare group nicknamed “Sandworm,” linked to the GRU, Russia’s military intelligence agency. Andy Greenberg traces their campaigns from early disruptions in Ukraine—like shutting down power grids in 2015 and 2016—to the release of NotPetya in 2017, the most destructive cyberattack in history, which crippled global companies, hospitals, and infrastructure. Through interviews with security researchers, intelligence officials, and victims, Greenberg shows how Sandworm pioneered a new kind of hybrid war: using malware, worms, and supply chain attacks as weapons of state power. He situates these attacks within the broader geopolitics of Russian aggression and highlights how poorly prepared the world remains for cyber conflict. The book reveals how cyberweapons can cause physical, economic, and political damage on a global scale, blurring the line between war and peace.

books.title: Sapiens
books.summary: Sapiens traces the history of Homo sapiens from their emergence in Africa to their dominance of the planet, organised around three major revolutions. The Cognitive Revolution (about 70,000 years ago) enabled humans to imagine, communicate complex ideas, and build shared myths that allowed large-scale cooperation. The Agricultural Revolution (about 12,000 years ago) created surpluses and civilisations but also entrenched hierarchy, inequality, and harder lives for many. The Scientific Revolution (about 500 years ago) unleashed discovery, capitalism, and technology, driving unprecedented growth and human control over nature, but also new dangers like imperialism, ecological collapse, and nuclear war. Harari shows how much of human order—nations, money, religion, laws—rests on shared fictions that enable large-scale coordination. The book ends by asking what future revolutions in biotechnology and artificial intelligence may mean for redefining what it is to be human.

books.title: Savarkar and the Making of Hindutva
books.summary: A critical biography of Vinayak Damodar Savarkar, the controversial nationalist who laid the ideological foundation of Hindutva. Drawing on archival research, Bakhle examines his evolution from a revolutionary anti-colonial activist—imprisoned by the British for armed resistance—to a political thinker whose writings, especially Hindutva: Who Is a Hindu?, reframed Indian identity in religious and cultural terms. She highlights the contradictions in his life: an atheist who championed a religiously defined nationalism, a prisoner seeking clemency while inspiring radical youth, and a modernist who also legitimized exclusionary politics. The book situates Savarkar within the currents of global nationalism, colonial modernity, and Indian politics, showing how his ideas, though divisive, became central to India’s contemporary political landscape.

books.title: Sayed Haider Raza
books.summary: A biography of one of modern India's greatest painters, a founding member of the Progressive Artists' Group who spent much of his life in Paris before returning to India in his final years. Art historian Yashodhara Dalmia traces Raza's journey from his childhood in the forests of Madhya Pradesh to international acclaim, following his artistic evolution toward his signature meditative geometry of the bindu, alongside his friendships, his marriage to the French artist Janine Mongillat, and his personal life.

books.title: Scale
books.summary: Scale explores the hidden mathematical laws that govern growth, sustainability, and collapse across biology, cities, and corporations. Organisms—from mice to elephants—follow predictable scaling laws: metabolic rates, lifespans, and growth all scale with body size in precise ratios. This also applies to human systems: cities follow “superlinear” scaling (as they grow, they become disproportionately more productive, innovative, and wealth-generating but also face greater crime and disease), while companies tend to follow “sublinear” scaling, meaning they grow, stagnate, and eventually die. Scaling laws as universal principles, offering insight into sustainability, urban growth, and humanity’s future in the face of environmental and resource pressures.

books.title: Scamlands
books.summary: An investigative journey into Asia's booming fraud economy, tracing the networks of deceit from the rural heartland of eastern India to the scam compounds of Southeast Asia. Poonam follows the people who make and are made by these operations, arguing that the scams reshaping economies thrive on inequality, technological change, and eroding trust—and that, for many, fraud has become less an aberration than an expression of agency and ingenuity.

books.title: Science and the State
books.summary: Gascoigne traces the history of the relationship between science and the state from the Scientific Revolution through World War II, showing how modern science and modern statecraft emerged together, each reinforcing the other. He argues that the evolving functions of states (war, administration, regulation) created a space for science to grow (funding, institutional authority, mission), while science, in turn, enhanced the capabilities, legitimacy, and reach of states. The alliance that formed by mid-20th century, especially during wartime, laid the foundations for contemporary science-state interdependence.

books.title: Secret Lives of Color
books.summary:
The fascinating stories behind 75 colors, dyes, and hues that have shaped art, culture, and history. The book reveals how colors are far more than just visual experiences—they are deeply intertwined with human creativity, commerce, and even politics.

Organized into chapters by color families—such as red, blue, yellow, green, and purple—St. Clair delves into the historical, cultural, and scientific significance of each shade. 

**Carmine (Cochenille)**: Made from crushed cochineal insects, this deep red dye was a symbol of wealth and status in Europe during the Renaissance. It was highly sought after for textiles and paintings

**Vermilion**: A bright, orange-red pigment derived from the mineral cinnabar. Used in ancient China and later by European artists, vermilion was prized but also toxic due to its mercury content.

**Ultramarine**: Derived from lapis lazuli, this rich, vibrant blue was so expensive that it was reserved for the robes of the Virgin Mary in medieval and Renaissance art. Its cost sometimes dictated the composition of entire paintings.

**Prussian Blue**: Accidentally discovered in the 18th century, this synthetic pigment became widely used for its affordability and vibrant hue. It was also used in engineering blueprints, giving them their iconic name.

**Indian Yellow**: A warm, golden-yellow pigment rumored to be made from the urine of cows fed only on mango leaves. This exotic origin has been debated, but the pigment was highly valued by European artists.

**Naples Yellow**: One of the oldest synthetic pigments, used by ancient Egyptians and Romans. It contains lead, making it both vibrant and hazardous.

**Scheele’s Green**: A bright, toxic green pigment that contained arsenic. Popular in wallpapers during the 18th and 19th centuries, it was later linked to health issues, including the suspected poisoning of Napoleon Bonaparte.

**Verdigris**: Derived from copper, this blue-green pigment was widely used in art and architecture. However, it was highly unstable and would often fade or react with other pigments.

**Tyrian Purple**: Known as the "color of kings," this dye was extracted from the glands of sea snails. Its production was labor-intensive and expensive, making it a luxury reserved for royalty and high officials.

**Mauveine**: The first synthetic dye, discovered in 1856 by William Perkin, revolutionized the textile industry. This pale purple became a fashion sensation and marked the beginning of modern chemistry in dyes.

**Bone Black**: Made by charring animal bones, this deep black was used in ancient art and continues to be a staple in painting.

**Lamp Black**: Produced from soot, it was one of the earliest pigments used by humans, appearing in prehistoric cave paintings.

**Lead White**: A key ingredient in oil painting for centuries, lead white provided a brilliant, opaque finish but was highly toxic. Artists like Rembrandt relied on it for its unique texture and color properties.

**Titanium White**: Introduced in the 20th century, this pigment replaced lead white as a safer, brighter alternative and remains widely used today.

books.title: Seven Brief Lessons on Physics
books.summary: Seven Brief Lessons on Physics distils modern physics into seven short essays that explain the most important scientific ideas of the 20th century and their implications. It begins with Einstein’s general relativity, showing how space and time are dynamic and intertwined, and moves to quantum mechanics, where uncertainty and probability govern the smallest scales. Rovelli then discusses the cosmos, from black holes to the Big Bang, and the atomic structure of matter, linking it to the probabilistic nature of quantum fields. He explores the role of heat, entropy, and the arrow of time, and describes the unification of forces and particles through quantum field theory. Finally, he turns to humanity’s place in this universe, connecting the workings of the brain and consciousness to physical laws. The book concludes by emphasising that scientific knowledge is provisional, ever-evolving, and deeply intertwined with our attempt to understand reality.

books.title: Several Short Sentences About Writing
books.summary: Several Short Sentences About Writing* challenges conventional writing advice (topic sentences, outlines, rigid structure, prescriptive rules), arguing that much of what we believe helps writing actually constrains it. It emphasizes listening, noticing, and working sentence by sentence; writing as a process of thought; trusting the reader; and finding clarity through simplicity and awareness rather than through formula.

books.title: Sex Robots & Vegan Meat
books.summary: Sex Robots & Vegan Meat explores four cutting-edge technologies—sex robots, lab-grown (vegan) meat, artificial wombs, and euthanasia pods—and the people pushing them forward. Kleeman reports on lifelike, AI-powered sexbots designed for companionship or erotic use; cultured meat startups aiming to replace traditional animal farming; experiments in growing fetuses outside the human body; and self-operated death machines. Jenny Kleeman argues these innovations are driven by convenience, profit, and often male-centric visions, raising ethical and societal questions about humanity, intimacy, reproduction, sustenance, and mortality.

books.title: Shattered Lands
books.summary: Shattered Lands traces how the vast “Indian Empire” unraveled into a dozen modern states through five decisive partitions—administrative breakaways in the late 1930s (such as Burma and Aden), the 1947 division of India and Pakistan, the detachment of the Gulf from Indian oversight, and the 1971 creation of Bangladesh—arguing that borders emerged from hasty, top-down choices made amid imperial retreat, war, and crisis rather than from timeless national destinies. Sam Dalrymple blends archival research with on-the-ground testimonies to show how bureaucratic improvisation, elite bargaining, and colonial cartography collided with mass displacement, communal violence, and long aftershocks for minorities; he challenges nationalist stories that back-project inevitability onto contingent events and highlights how these partitions continue to shape security, migration, and identity across South Asia and the Gulf. His conclusion is that remembering the messy, contingent making of these frontiers is essential to resisting mythmaking and to designing more humane policies for today’s border conflicts.

books.title: She Has Her Mothers Laugh
books.summary: A wide-ranging exploration of heredity, tracing how humans have understood, shaped, and misinterpreted inheritance across history, from ancient ideas of bloodlines and family traits to modern genetics and CRISPR. Zimmer examines heredity not just as the transmission of genes but as a cultural and social phenomenon—covering topics like how childhood traits were once linked to morality, the legacy of eugenics, the role of epigenetics and microbiomes, and the ethical implications of genetic engineering. He shows how heredity is neither deterministic nor limited to DNA, but a dynamic interplay of biology, environment, and culture, constantly reshaping who we are and what we pass on. The book ultimately argues that the old notion of heredity as a rigid, linear force has given way to a more complex, nuanced understanding of how identities and traits are formed and carried forward.

books.title: Six Degrees
books.summary: Six Degrees: The Science of a Connected Age examines the science of networks, explaining how seemingly small, local interactions can generate large-scale patterns across society, biology, and technology. Drawing on examples from the spread of diseases, the functioning of the internet, corporate structures, and social movements, Watts shows how networks follow certain mathematical principles that determine their robustness, vulnerability, and capacity for rapid information or contagion flow. He builds on the “small world” concept—popularized by the idea of six degrees of separation—to reveal that many complex systems share common underlying structures, whether social, biological, or technological. The book argues that understanding these principles allows us to predict and sometimes even control how innovations, behaviors, or crises ripple across the world.

books.title: Some Assembly Required
books.summary: Some Assembly Required traces the hidden history of evolution by showing how dramatic innovations in life—such as the emergence of limbs, feathers, eyes, and even complex behaviors—were built from ancient genetic and molecular parts already present in earlier organisms. Shubin explains how breakthroughs in molecular biology and genetics, particularly the discovery of “toolkit genes” like Hox genes, revealed that the same genetic switches and developmental pathways operate across diverse species, from worms to humans. Through examples ranging from the evolution of lungs in fish to the rise of warm-blooded mammals, the book demonstrates that evolution is less about inventing new features from scratch and more about repurposing existing biological systems. By blending fossil evidence with molecular discoveries, Shubin argues that the story of life is one of continuity, where radical change emerges from reusing and reassembling old parts in new ways.

books.title: Something Deeply Hidden
books.summary: Something Deeply Hidden argues that the best explanation for the mysteries of quantum mechanics is the Everett or “many-worlds” interpretation, which posits that all possible outcomes of quantum events actually occur, each in its own branching universe. Carroll begins by laying out the measurement problem—the unresolved question of how and why a wave function collapse seems to occur in standard quantum mechanics—and shows why conventional interpretations like Copenhagen or hidden-variable theories fail to provide a consistent picture. He then explains how the many-worlds framework eliminates the need for collapse, treating the wave function as real and universal, while quantum branching naturally accounts for probabilities and observations. The book also explores how this view connects to cosmology, spacetime, and the search for a theory of quantum gravity, suggesting that embracing many-worlds not only clarifies quantum puzzles but also opens new paths for physics.

books.title: Space, Time and Motion
books.summary: The first volume of Carroll's "Biggest Ideas in the Universe" series, covering the physics of classical mechanics and relativity while not shying away from the actual mathematics. Carroll walks readers through concepts like force, energy, spacetime, and Einstein's theories, aiming to give a genuine working understanding of how physicists describe the universe rather than mere metaphors.

books.title: Space. Life. Matter.
books.summary: Space. Life. Matter. traces the story of modern science in India through the lives and work of its pioneering scientists. Covering figures such as C.V. Raman, Homi Bhabha, Vikram Sarabhai, Obaid Siddiqi, and others, the book shows how their vision and institution-building efforts laid the foundations for India’s achievements in physics, space exploration, molecular biology, and materials science. Pulakkat situates their work within the context of newly independent India, highlighting how these scientists balanced world-class research with the national imperative of self-reliance, often working with limited resources but immense creativity. The narrative weaves together personal histories, scientific breakthroughs, and institutional milestones to show how these individuals transformed India’s scientific landscape, creating enduring legacies in research and innovation.

books.title: Steve Jobs
books.summary: A comprehensive biography of Apple’s co-founder, based on more than forty interviews with Jobs and over a hundred with colleagues, family, and rivals. It follows his life from his adoption and youth in California, through founding Apple, his ouster, and triumphant return that led to the creation of transformative products like the iMac, iPod, iPhone, and iPad. Isaacson portrays Jobs as a visionary with an obsession for design, simplicity, and perfection, whose “reality distortion field” pushed teams beyond their limits but also made him volatile, manipulative, and often cruel. The book explores his influence on personal computing, music, phones, digital publishing, and animation through Pixar, while also delving into his struggles with relationships and illness. Ultimately, it presents Jobs as a man who fused technology and the liberal arts to shape the digital age.

books.title: Supremacy
books.summary: An account of the race to build artificial general intelligence, told through the rival ambitions of DeepMind's Demis Hassabis and OpenAI's Sam Altman and the two idealists' entanglement with the giants Google and Microsoft. Olson charts how founders who set out to build AI safely and for humanity's benefit ended up absorbed into a corporate contest for dominance, raising questions about power, money, and control over a technology that could reshape the world.

books.title: Surely You're Joking Mr Feynman
books.summary: A collection of autobiographical anecdotes from the Nobel Prize-winning physicist, ranging from cracking safes at Los Alamos during the Manhattan Project to picking locks, playing bongos, painting, and puzzling out the world with relentless curiosity. Less a scientific memoir than a portrait of a mind that refused to take anything on authority, it celebrates play, irreverence, and the joy of figuring things out for oneself.

books.title: Surveillance State
books.summary:
Under Xi Jinping, the Communist Party is turning the world’s largest population into both data source and data subject, marrying facial recognition, biometrics and AI scoring systems to a Leninist vision of social order. From the first chapter—set in Xinjiang, where “terror‑predictive” software weighs how often a Uyghur family uses its back door—the authors show how experimental policing zones have become blueprints for nationwide rollout._

_The book’s strength lies in vivid case studies. _We follow engineers building Hangzhou’s “City Brain,” a traffic‑control AI now repurposed for pandemic tracking; village cadres piloting the “Sharp Eyes” network, which turns public CCTV feeds into a reality‑TV‑style neighborhood watch; and parents coaxed into rating teachers on a blockchain ledger. Throughout, Chin and Lin balance technical explanation with human stories: a Uyghur entrepreneur who deletes jokes from his phone nightly, a Hangzhou coder proud that his system clears ambulances through red lights in seconds._

_The authors note that many Chinese citizens welcome cameras for crime prevention and digital contact tracing; privacy, one interviewee admits, “was never in the vocabulary” until recently. They trace how the Party invokes Confucian paternalism (“governing for the people, not by the people”) while quietly expanding databases that now hold voiceprints for 960 million individuals. Still, Chin and Lin show cracks in the façade: local hacks, public outcry after a data leak in Shanghai, and academics warning that algorithmic coercion can backfire by eroding trust.

books.title: Surveillance Valley
books.summary: Surveillance Valley argues that the internet was born not as a utopian innovation but as a tool for surveillance, rooted in U.S. military counterinsurgency efforts during the Vietnam War, with projects under ARPA designed to collect and analyse data to anticipate insurgent behaviour. Levine traces how this surveillance mindset persisted into the privatisation of the internet, as corporations like Google, Facebook, and Amazon capitalised on user data and formed deep ties with military and intelligence agencies. Even privacy-focused tools like Tor and Signal, often seen as resistance technologies, were funded in ways that may have served surveillance purposes. The book portrays the modern internet as an extension of a “military-digital complex,” where tech giants function as surveillance arms of state power. Levine ultimately warns that the internet was weaponised by design and remains fundamentally structured for control and extraction, not liberation.

books.title: System Error
books.summary:
The authors—a philosopher, a computer scientist, and a policymaker—team up to analyze how the tech industry has steered society into an era of unprecedented innovation, but also deep ethical, political, and societal dilemmas. Drawing on their experience as Stanford professors, they unpack the forces driving Big Tech's rise and explore how its unchecked growth has shaped everything from privacy to democracy._

_The book identifies key issues such as:_

- _**Optimization Without Ethics**: How Silicon Valley's focus on efficiency and profit often overlooks broader consequences, like the erosion of privacy or the spread of misinformation._
- _**Algorithmic Bias**: The ways in which AI systems can perpetuate and amplify societal inequalities._
- _**Tech’s Impact on Democracy**: How platforms like Facebook and YouTube have disrupted public discourse, enabling polarization and the spread of extremist views.

books.title: Talk to Me
books.summary: About the rise of voice technology—virtual assistants like Siri, Alexa, and Google Assistant—and its implications for society. The book traces the history of speech recognition and natural language processing, explains the technological breakthroughs that made conversational AI possible, and profiles the companies and researchers driving the field. Vlahos highlights both the opportunities—more natural human-computer interaction, accessibility for the disabled, hands-free convenience—and the risks, including surveillance, loss of privacy, and growing dependence on corporate-controlled ecosystems. He also reflects on his personal project creating a “Dadbot” to preserve his dying father’s voice and stories, illustrating the emotional power of conversational interfaces. Ultimately, the book argues that voice will become a dominant interface, reshaping technology’s role in daily life and raising urgent ethical and social questions.

books.title: Tata
books.summary: The 150-year history of the Tata Group, shows how it grew from a 19th-century family-owned trading firm into India’s most influential business conglomerate with global reach. The book explores how the Tatas strategically balanced profit with philanthropy, embedding themselves in India’s nation-building project through ventures in steel, power, aviation, IT, and consumer goods. Raianu highlights how the company cultivated a reputation for trust and social responsibility, while also navigating the tensions of globalisation, liberalisation, and family governance. By examining the Tatas’ relationships with the colonial state, independent India, and international markets, the book argues that the group helped shape both Indian capitalism and India’s global economic identity.

books.title: Techno-Nationalism
books.summary: Techno-Nationalism argues that advanced technology—especially semiconductors and AI—has become inseparable from national security, economic sovereignty, and [[geopolitical]] leverage, driving governments to weaponize supply chains, impose export controls, reshore production, and build tight public–private tech alliances in order to contain rivals and secure strategic advantage. Capri shows how the U.S.–China rivalry has turned critical technologies into instruments of statecraft: Washington uses sanctions, entity lists, investment screening, and industrial policy (CHIPS-style subsidization, ring-fenced supply chains) to deny Beijing access to high-end capabilities, while China pursues self-sufficiency through state-backed initiatives like Made in China 2025 and indigenous capacity-building in fabs, 5G, and AI. He frames this as a systemic shift away from the old model of globalized, efficiency-optimized value chains toward fragmented, bloc-aligned “trusted networks,” in which supply chain resilience and ideological alignment matter more than cost. The book concludes that this techno-nationalist order will define not only trade and manufacturing but also diplomacy, narrative warfare, and societal stability, forcing governments, firms, and even midsize countries to choose sides and build redundancy for a world of permanent strategic competition.

books.title: Technology and the Rise of Great Powers
books.summary: An argument that the nations which come to dominate an era are not those that first invent a breakthrough technology but those that most successfully diffuse it across their whole economy. Drawing on the histories of the Industrial Revolutions, Ding develops a "GPT diffusion" theory of general-purpose technologies and applies it to today's contest over artificial intelligence between the United States and China.

books.title: The Afterlife of Data
books.summary: The Afterlife of Data examines what should happen to the vast troves of digital traces people leave behind when they die—social-media profiles, chats, photos, biometrics, location trails—and argues that these “digital remains” demand the same moral consideration as bodies and estates. Carl Öhman shows how today’s defaults (platform terms of service, patchy inheritance laws, and commercial incentives) leave families, platforms, and researchers negotiating ownership, consent, memorialization, and deletion in an ad-hoc way that risks exploitation, erasure, or both. Moving across cases—from dormant profiles at planetary scale to AI systems trained on the dead’s data—he weighs the cultural value of preserving records against privacy and dignity, critiques proposals that treat data as pure property, and advances a governance framework grounded in personhood, fiduciary stewardship (e.g., digital executors and duties of care), due process, and plural institutions (including public-interest archives) rather than a single global authority. He concludes that societies must deliberately design legal, technical, and institutional rules for digital death so grief, memory, research, and rights are protected over the long term.

books.title: The Age of AI
books.summary: Explores how artificial intelligence is transforming human knowledge, perception, and power in ways comparable to the Enlightenment or the invention of the printing press. The authors argue that AI’s ability to generate knowledge beyond human comprehension challenges our traditional frameworks of reason, ethics, and governance, forcing societies to rethink concepts such as truth, agency, and responsibility. Through examples from science, defense, and geopolitics, they show how AI systems already act autonomously in domains once limited to human judgment, reshaping how individuals, institutions, and nations understand and act upon the world. The book concludes by urging the development of philosophical and ethical foundations to guide humanity through this epistemic revolution before its consequences outpace our capacity to manage them.

books.title: The Age of Extraction
books.summary: An account of how a handful of dominant technology platforms have become among the most effective instruments of wealth extraction ever built, seizing money, data, and attention while deepening inequality and eroding the democratic promise the early internet once carried. Wu traces how the open web of the 1990s curdled into concentrated economic power, and lays out proposals—drawing on antimonopoly history, AI, and crypto—for rebalancing the economy toward broad prosperity.

books.title: The Age of Living Machines
books.summary: A compelling vision of a new technological revolution—**Convergence 2.0**—where engineering and biology unite to spark innovations with as much transformative power as the digital breakthroughs of the 20th century. The book showcases emerging biotechnologies—like virus-built batteries, protein-based water filters, cancer-detecting nanoparticles, mind-reading prosthetics, and engineered crops—that promise to address global challenges such as energy, food, water scarcity, and health care. Hockfield frames this wave amidst a backdrop of growing global crises, suggesting that only bold investment in basic research, interdisciplinary collaboration, and institutional support can bring these solutions to scale. Drawing inspiration from MIT’s convergence approach over history, she argues we stand on the cusp of a biological era that can redefine our future—if we consciously choose to build it.

books.title: The Age of Surveillance Capitalism
books.summary: A sweeping critique of an economic order in which companies like Google and Facebook claim human experience as free raw material, translating our behavior into data used to predict and increasingly to shape what we do. Zuboff argues this "surveillance capitalism" represents a new and unprecedented form of power that threatens autonomy and democracy itself, and traces its mechanisms, logic, and consequences in exhaustive detail.

books.title: The Anarchist in the Library
books.summary: An exploration of the twenty-first-century struggle over information, framed as a clash between total freedom (anarchy) and total control (oligarchy). Vaidhyanathan identifies the peer-to-peer network as the defining structure of the age, ranging across copyright wars, Napster, hackers, libraries, political dissent, and even terrorist "leaderless resistance" to show how battles over the flow of information are reshaping culture and politics.

books.title: The Anarchy
books.summary: The dramatic rise of the British East India Company from a small trading enterprise to the dominant power in India between the mid-18th and early 19th centuries. Dalrymple details how the company exploited political fragmentation in the Mughal Empire, using military force, financial manipulation, and alliances to gain territorial control, culminating in the conquest of Bengal and beyond. He emphasizes the unprecedented nature of a private corporation wielding sovereign power—raising armies, collecting taxes, and ruling vast territories—while its shareholders in London profited from Indian revenues. The narrative highlights the devastation caused by extractive policies, including famine and economic collapse, and argues that the East India Company pioneered a form of corporate colonialism that reshaped both India and the global economy.

books.title: The Art of Freedom
books.summary: The Art of Freedom is a thoroughly researched and richly detailed biography that restores Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay—multi-faceted activist, institution builder, and feminist—to her rightful place in modern Indian history. Nicolae Slate draws on previously unpublished papers and journals to offer insight into her striking life arc: from child widowhood and artistic pursuits, to active leadership in the freedom movement, to her pivotal roles post-independence in refugee rehabilitation (founding Faridabad), arts and crafts revival, and the creation of cultural institutions like the Sangeet Natak Akademi, National School of Drama, and Central Cottage Industries Emporium. Slate captures her complexity: a passionate advocate of women’s participation (once challenging Gandhi to include women in the Dandi March), a radical thinker comfortable confronting allies, and a resilient reformer whose personal struggles only deepened her political work.

books.title: The Backstage of Democracy
books.summary: The Backstage of Democracy examines how Indian election campaigns have transformed over the last decade with the rise of political consultants, data analytics, and strategic communication. Sharma shows that parties rely increasingly on professional teams—pollsters, digital strategists, consultants, and social-media volunteers—to shape campaign messaging and voter mobilisation. This shift is not just technological but reflects deeper changes in party power structures, notions of political expertise, and citizens' roles in democracy. Using empirical data and ethnographic insight, the book explores these sweeping changes within parties like the Congress and BJP, tracks the growth of the consulting industry, and analyses the implications such professionalisation has for democratic norms, accountability, and the broader political culture.

books.title: The Battle for your Brain
books.summary: A survey of the emerging neurotechnologies—brain-scanning wearables, neural implants, and decoding devices—that are beginning to make our thoughts and mental states readable and manipulable by employers, governments, and companies. Farahany, a legal scholar and ethicist, argues for a new right to "cognitive liberty," warning that mental privacy and freedom of thought may be the next frontier we have to defend.

books.title: The Beginning of Infinity
books.summary: A wide-ranging work of scientific philosophy arguing that good explanations—those hard to vary and with genuine reach—are the engine of unlimited human progress. Deutsch draws on physics, epistemology, evolution, and the theory of computation to make the case that knowledge can grow without bound, and that there are no inherent limits to what people, armed with the right explanations, can eventually understand and achieve.

books.title: The Big Nine
books.summary: The Big Nine examines how artificial intelligence is being shaped by nine powerful companies—Amazon, Google, Facebook, Apple, IBM, and Microsoft in the United States, and Baidu, Alibaba, and Tencent in China—and how their competing incentives are steering the future of AI. Webb argues that the American firms, driven by short-term profit motives and shareholder pressure, often prioritize speed and consumer applications, while the Chinese firms operate under state direction, focusing on long-term national power and control. Through scenario planning, she outlines optimistic, pragmatic, and catastrophic futures for AI depending on how governments, corporations, and societies act today, warning that without coordinated global governance and strategic foresight, AI could reinforce inequality, erode human rights, and centralize power in ways that are hard to reverse. The book ultimately calls for urgent collective action to align AI development with human values and long-term societal interests.

books.title: The Billionaire Raj
books.summary: Billionaire Raj examines the rise of India’s super-rich elite and how their wealth has reshaped the country’s politics, economy, and society. It traces the transformation from India’s state-led socialist era to the liberalisation of the 1990s, which unleashed entrepreneurial ambition but also fostered crony capitalism, weak regulation, and vast inequality. Through profiles of industrialists, tycoons, and politicians, Crabtree highlights how fortunes were built through opaque deals, resource grabs, and connections, creating an oligarchic “Billionaire Raj” that mirrors the excesses of America’s Gilded Age. The book argues that while this surge of wealth demonstrates India’s economic potential, it also risks undermining democracy and inclusive growth unless reforms curb corruption, strengthen institutions, and ensure fairer distribution of prosperity.

books.title: The Body
books.summary: The Body: A Guide for Occupants is a tour through the human body, explaining its structure, functions, and quirks in accessible detail. Bryson moves systematically from head to toe, covering organs, systems, and processes—from the brain and nervous system to digestion, immunity, and reproduction—while weaving in medical history, scientific discoveries, and the limits of what we still do not understand. He highlights the body’s resilience and efficiency, but also its fragility and susceptibility to disease, as well as the role of medicine and public health in extending human life. The book concludes that despite centuries of study, the body remains a source of awe, mystery, and wonder, reminding us of both our biological ingenuity and our inherent vulnerability.

books.title: The Bomb, the Bank, the Mullah and the Poppies
books.summary: The Bomb, the Bank, the Mullah and the Poppies traces how Pakistan’s deep state—its military, intelligence agencies, and political elites—leveraged clandestine means to build a nuclear arsenal and strengthen state power. Malhotra examines how Zulfikar Ali Bhutto initiated the nuclear programme and reportedly used Agha Hasan Abedi’s BCCI (Bank of Credit and Commerce International) to channel funds—even from illicit sources like drug cartels—for strategic ends.
