He delves into how the narcotics trade (“poppies”) and covert financial networks prop up nuclear ambitions, migrant alliances, and regional proxies, including support for the Taliban under Generals Zia-ul-Haq and Musharraf. Blending historical research and forensic detail, the book reveals how deceptive statecraft, drug trafficking, and ideological patronage created a “narco-nuclear” Pakistan—a country that projected helplessness publicly while orchestrating power and influence in the shadows.

books.title: The Book of Why
books.summary: The Book of Why explains how the science of causality has advanced beyond mere statistical correlation to a structured framework for understanding cause-and-effect. Judea Pearl traces this evolution through tools like causal diagrams (directed acyclic graphs) and his “ladder of causation”: (1) association (observing patterns), (2) intervention (understanding what happens if we act), and (3) counterfactuals (imagining what would have happened otherwise). He shows how this framework allows researchers to answer previously unresolvable questions—about medicine, economics, and social science—by distinguishing between correlation and genuine causation. Pearl also critiques the limitations of purely data-driven machine learning, arguing that true artificial intelligence requires causal reasoning, not just pattern recognition.

books.title: The Book
books.summary: The history of the book through its four essential elements—paper, ink, writing, and binding. Houston explores how each component developed across civilizations: from papyrus scrolls in Egypt and parchment in Europe to the invention of paper in China; from ancient inks and scripts to movable type and Gutenberg’s press; and from hand-bound manuscripts to industrial printing. Along the way, he shows how technological advances, cultural exchanges, and economic forces shaped the evolution of books into the familiar codex form we use today. The narrative underscores the book as both a technological artefact and a cultural symbol that has carried knowledge across millennia and continues to adapt in the digital age.-

books.title: The Brandeis-Frankfurter Connection
books.summary: The Brandeis/Frankfurter Connection investigates how U.S. Supreme Court Justice Louis Brandeis and his protégé Felix Frankfurter, later also a Justice, covertly influenced American politics, policy, and public opinion during the early to mid-20th century. The book documents how Brandeis, despite judicial ethics that required judges to remain above politics, secretly funnelled money, ideas, and guidance to Frankfurter, who acted as his intermediary with politicians, journalists, academics, and activist groups. Through this channel, Brandeis advanced progressive causes—such as labour rights, Zionism, and economic regulation—while maintaining the appearance of judicial impartiality. Murphy concludes that this hidden partnership blurred the lines between judicial independence and political advocacy, raising enduring questions about judicial ethics and the proper limits of a Justice’s role in public life.

books.title: The Bullet Journal Method
books.summary: The definitive book on the Bullet Journal method of productivity. Not really my style so I am going to consign this to the back recesses of my knowledge base.

books.title: The Burning Earth
books.summary: A magisterial global environmental history of roughly the last five hundred years, tracing how the pursuit of profit, powered by new energy sources and technologies, has reshaped the planet and driven migration, conquest, and ecological destruction. Amrith insists that all history is environmental history, weaving together the story of human societies and the natural world they have transformed and been transformed by.

books.title: The Chipko Movement - A People's History
books.summary: The Chipko Movement: A People’s History reexamines the iconic forest conservation movement not through the lens of its famous leaders like Chandi Prasad Bhatt or Sunderlal Bahuguna, but through the lives and sacrifices of ordinary villagers—men, women, and children—who sustained its grassroots power. Pathak draws on decades of archival research, oral testimonies, and historical context to show how Chipko was deeply rooted in local culture, livelihoods, and ecological interdependence, challenging the mythologised narratives that have dominated popular memory. The book emphasises the movement’s broader significance: as a people’s history, it brings into sharp focus how the movement was shaped by everyday resistance, social inequality, and collective agency rather than by singular environmental figures.

books.title: The Code Breaker
books.summary: The Code Breaker_ by Walter Isaacson tells the story of Jennifer Doudna and the development of CRISPR gene-editing technology, situating her work within the larger scientific race to understand and manipulate the code of life. The book traces Doudna’s early fascination with biology, her breakthroughs in RNA research, and her central role in the discovery that CRISPR could be harnessed to edit genes with unprecedented precision. Isaacson explores the fierce rivalries, collaborations, and ethical debates surrounding CRISPR—from patent battles to its potential uses in curing diseases, altering embryos, and even enhancing humans. The narrative also reflects on how biotechnology is becoming the defining scientific revolution of our time, comparable to the digital and physics revolutions of the past century.

books.title: The Colonial Constitution
books.summary: The Colonial Constitution argues that India’s Constitution, though celebrated as a product of independence, carries deep continuities with colonial governance that continue to shape the Republic. Sengupta traces how the British used law and constitutional instruments—such as the Government of India Acts—to centralise power, entrench executive dominance, and prioritise order over liberty. He shows that the framers of the Indian Constitution, while seeking to build a democratic republic, retained many of these colonial features, particularly a powerful central executive, weak checks and balances, and an overriding emphasis on state authority. The book contends that this legacy explains many contemporary challenges in Indian democracy, from curbs on civil liberties to excessive state control, suggesting that true constitutional reform requires confronting and dismantling these colonial continuities.

books.title: The Color of North
books.summary: Fabulous book on various strange and wonderful proteins and what it takes to make them. Very interesting take on how the body makes these proteins and how it will be useful to us. Also interesting from Dhruv's perspective.

books.title: The Coming Wave
books.summary: The Coming Wave describes how two rapidly advancing technologies—artificial intelligence and synthetic biology—are converging to reshape humanity’s future. Mustafa Suleyman draws on his experience founding DeepMind and leading Inflection AI to illustrate how these technologies offer unprecedented promise—for personalized medicine, automation, abundant intelligence, and innovative solutions to global challenges—while also introducing extreme risks, such as engineered pandemics, surveillance states, autonomous weapons, and destabilized governments. He emphasizes that unlike past revolutions, this wave is omnipresent, evolving, and hard to regulate. Suleyman proposes a concept he calls the “containment problem”—the existential challenge of governing powerful technologies we willingly adopt, by designing safeguards, regulation, and cultural strategies before it's too late.

books.title: The Confidence Game
books.summary: On the psychology of con artists and why people fall for frauds, scams, and swindles. Drawing on research in psychology, neuroscience, and behavioural economics, Konnikova dissects the “long con” into its stages—from the “put-up” (identifying a mark) to the “pay-off” (extracting money or trust)—and explains how con artists exploit universal human traits like empathy, trust, hope, and the desire for meaning. Through vivid case studies of famous scams, she shows that susceptibility is not limited to the gullible but is rooted in the very cognitive and emotional mechanisms that make social life possible. The book concludes that while cons expose human vulnerability, they also reveal how our capacity for belief and trust is essential for cooperation and progress.

books.title: The Constitution of Knowledge
books.summary: The Constitution of Knowledge explores how liberal societies create objective truth through a decentralised system of rules, norms, and institutions that is akin to a “constitution of knowledge.” Just as political constitutions channel conflict into structured debate, the institutions of science, journalism, law, and academia channel disagreement into a collective process of verification that produces shared knowledge. This system is under threat from disinformation, conspiracy theories, cancel culture, and authoritarian manipulation, which undermine trust in the truth-seeking process. The survival of liberal democracy depends on defending the norms of free inquiry, pluralism, and institutionalised critical checking, even when uncomfortable or unpopular.

books.title: The Cooking of Books
books.summary: Ramachandra Guha’s deeply personal literary memoir that chronicles the remarkable four-decade-long intellectual and emotional relationship between himself and his editor, Rukun Advani. Through candid letters, emails, and anecdotes, Guha traces their unlikely friendship—from their disparate college personas at St. Stephen’s College, to the transformative editorial collaboration at Oxford University Press that shaped Guha’s narrative voice in works on environment, cricket, and Indian history. The memoir reveals how Advani, with his sharp wit and literary acumen, helped refine Guha's ideas, while their fraught debates on politics and scholarship added depth to their bond. Set against the backdrop of a changing publishing landscape, the book also critiques the corporatization of literary culture, lamenting how the art of careful editing has been overshadowed by marketing cycles. More than a memoir, it’s a tribute to an editor’s indispensable, often unsung, role in shaping ideas and a celebration of enduring intellectual camaraderie.

books.title: The Corporation in the Twenty-First Century
books.summary: The Corporation in the Twenty-First Century offers a sharp, insightful reevaluation of modern business. John Kay argues that traditional notions—like the importance of physical capital, factory ownership, and profit as the primary corporate purpose—have been displaced in today’s knowledge economy. He traces how companies have become “hollow”: they no longer own means of production; instead, workers operate remotely, capital is outsourced as a service, and authority stems from managerial expertise rather than ownership. Kay debunks the dominance of profit-maximization logic and the shareholder-value dogma, noting that these ideas often served financiers more than actual businesses and contributed to institutional failures like GE and Deutsche Bank. He emphasizes a shift toward intellectual capital, collaboration, and problem-solving, with successful firms like Apple and Meta thriving on these principles. Kay also highlights the crisis of trust experienced by modern corporations—while society adores their products, it distrusts the producers—and calls for expanding our understanding of capital to include social, human, and natural dimensions.

books.title: The Cost of Connection
books.summary: An argument that the mass harvesting of personal data amounts to a new form of colonialism—"data colonialism"—in which human life itself is annexed as raw material for capitalist extraction, much as land and labor were in earlier eras. The authors trace the historical parallels and the emerging social order this produces, and call for resistance to the normalization of continuous tracking.

books.title: The Creative Act
books.summary:
An exploration of the creative process, delving into the very essence of artistic identity. This is a must-read for anyone seeking to unlock their full creative potential. Rubin's insights are not limited to the realm of art, music, or literature; instead, they transcend genres, speaking to the universal human experience of creativity.

Rubin argues that creativity is not the exclusive domain of artists, but rather an innate aspect of the human experience. This perspective liberates readers from the notion that only a select few are capable of creative expression. By recognizing that creativity is an inherent part of our being, we can tap into its transformative power, allowing it to guide us on our personal and professional paths. Rubin doesn't so much provide a formula for success, but rather says we must embrace the uncertainty and messiness that accompanies the creative process. He encourages readers to surrender to their instincts, to trust in their inner voice, and to allow themselves to be fully immersed in the creative act. 

Rubin reminds us that creativity is a journey, not a destination, and that the most meaningful artistic expressions often arise from a place of uncertainty. By embracing this uncertainty, we can tap into a sense of curiosity and wonder, allowing ourselves to explore new ideas, experiment with different mediums, and push the boundaries of our creative potential. Throughout the book, he draws upon his own experiences as a renowned music producer, sharing insights gleaned from his work with iconic artists such as the Beastie Boys, Red Hot Chili Peppers, and Johnny Cash. These anecdotes serve as powerful illustrations of the creative process in action, demonstrating the importance of collaboration, experimentation, and risk-taking.

books.title: The Curse of Bigness
books.summary:
The Curse of Bigness revives Louis Brandeis’s antitrust philosophy to argue that excessive corporate concentration endangers democracy as much as it distorts markets. Wu traces the history of antitrust enforcement from the Gilded Age and the breakup of monopolies like Standard Oil and AT&T to the retreat of enforcement in the late 20th century, when efficiency and consumer prices replaced concerns about power. He shows how today’s tech giants and financial conglomerates mirror the monopolists of the past, amassing not only economic dominance but also political influence. The book contends that restoring vigorous antitrust action is essential to curbing inequality, protecting competition, and safeguarding democratic institutions._

**_Concentrated corporate power is a political as well as economic threat, and only robust antitrust enforcement can preserve both fair markets and democracy.+

books.title: The Data Detective
books.summary: A guide to navigating the overwhelming swirl of statistics we encounter every day. Tim Harford lays out ten common-sense rules—like noticing your emotional bias (“Search Your Feelings”), checking how a claim feels against your own experience (“Ponder Your Personal Experience”), questioning vague or misleading definitions (“Avoid Premature Enumeration”), seeking broad context (“Step Back and Enjoy the View”), and insisting on transparency even when “the computer says no.” Each rule is brought to life with real-world examples—from art forgery that fooled experts to misleading income statistics—and backed by psychology and economics insights. Overall, the book teaches readers that statistics aren’t to be feared or blindly trusted—but must be approached with curiosity, clarity, and healthy skepticism, using both data and intuition to understand the world more accurately.

books.title: The Dig
books.summary: A work of reportage on Keeladi, the Tamil Nadu excavation site whose Iron Age findings have become one of India's most politically charged archaeological digs. Journalist Sowmiya Ashok blends travel writing and first-hand investigation—from Tamil Nadu to Harappan Rakhigarhi and the lost port of Muziris—to show how battles over science and evidence are entangled with contests over India's past and identity.

books.title: The Digital Republic
books.summary: The Digital Republic examines how digital technologies—especially big tech platforms, algorithms, and artificial intelligence—are reshaping power and politics, and argues for a new constitutional order for the digital age. Susskind shows how a handful of corporations exercise quasi-sovereign authority by controlling speech, commerce, and personal data, often without transparency or accountability. He critiques the inadequacy of traditional regulatory approaches and proposes principles for digital self-government: accountability, transparency, competition, and rights protection. The book outlines possible reforms—ranging from stronger antitrust enforcement to new institutions overseeing algorithms and online platforms—insisting that democratic societies must deliberately design rules to govern digital power rather than leaving it to private actors.

books.title: The Digital Silk Road
books.summary: The book argues that China's digital infrastructure ambitions, manifesting in the Digital Silk Road (DSR), pose significant [[geopolitical]] implications for the world, as China seeks to reshape global governance, norms, and power dynamics through digital means. The DSR is a critical component of China's Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), aiming to connect China with other parts of Asia, Europe, and Africa through digital infrastructure. China's digital ambitions are driven by a desire to overcome its "middle-income trap" and become a high-tech leader. The DSR has expanded to over 130 countries, with China investing heavily in digital infrastructure, including 5G networks, data centers, and e-commerce platforms. The DSR enables China to project power, influence global governance, and challenge existing norms and institutions.

books.title: The Eastern Gate
books.summary: A narrative history of India’s troubled and strategically vital Northeast region, examining its complex mix of ethnicity, insurgency, geopolitics, and development. The book traces the region’s history from colonial annexation and the drawing of arbitrary borders to post-independence neglect, insurgent movements, and fraught relations with the Indian state. Chakravarti explores the lived realities of conflict, militarisation, and identity politics, while situating the Northeast within larger dynamics of migration, resource exploitation, and cross-border ties with China, Myanmar, and Bangladesh. He argues that the region’s marginalisation has fueled cycles of alienation and unrest, and that India’s ability to integrate the Northeast—politically, economically, and culturally—will be central to its future stability and its role in Asia.

books.title: The Enchantment of Democracy and India
books.summary: An exploration of how democracy in India has taken root and endured despite the country’s vast poverty, social divisions, and history of authoritarian governance. Kaviraj argues that democracy in India is not merely a constitutional framework transplanted from the West but a deeply cultural and historical phenomenon shaped by colonial experiences, nationalist movements, and the pluralistic ethos of Indian society. He examines how practices of political participation, popular mobilisation, and the language of rights and equality have been absorbed into everyday life, creating a widespread “enchantment” with democracy even amid dysfunctions like corruption, weak institutions, and inequality. The book concludes that India’s democratic resilience lies in this cultural embedding of democratic values, even as the system remains fragile and contested.

books.title: The Ethical Algorithm
books.summary: On how algorithms, while powerful tools for decision-making, often generate unintended harms—such as privacy violations, discrimination, and unfair outcomes—and explores how these issues can be addressed through rigorous design. Ethics cannot simply be bolted onto technology after deployment; instead, algorithms must be engineered with formal guarantees of fairness, privacy, accountability, and transparency. The authors draw on examples from machine learning, data privacy, and game theory to show how principles like differential privacy, fairness constraints, and incentive-compatible design can mitigate risks without sacrificing performance. The book concludes that the future of AI and data science depends on embedding ethics directly into code, ensuring that technological progress aligns with social values.

books.title: The Etymologicon
books.summary: A playful, digressive tour through the hidden connections between English words, in which each short chapter's ending links to the next in an unbroken chain of etymological association. Forsyth delights in surprising origins and coincidences, showing how words drift, mutate, and connect across history in ways that are as entertaining as they are illuminating.

books.title: The Feared
books.summary: A set of interviews with eleven political prisoners in India—among them several of the accused in the Bhima Koregaon case, such as Sudha Bharadwaj, Anand Teltumbde, Varavara Rao, and Shoma Sen—along with their families. Kolhatkar documents the harsh realities of incarceration and the human face of those held behind bars, framing the book as both a call for prison reform and a testament to hope, solidarity, and survival.

books.title: The Fifth Risk
books.summary: The Fifth Risk_ by Michael Lewis investigates how the U.S. federal government manages enormous, often invisible responsibilities—such as nuclear safety, food security, weather forecasting, and energy research—and how these functions were imperiled during the Trump administration’s transition. Lewis profiles little-known agencies like the Department of Energy, USDA, and NOAA, showing how their work underpins national safety and daily life, while warning that neglect, political appointments of unqualified leaders, and disdain for expertise put the country at risk. The “fifth risk,” beyond the obvious dangers of nuclear accidents, terrorism, natural disasters, and economic collapse, is mismanagement—when government fails through ignorance or inattention. The book ultimately defends the value of competent, science-driven public service as essential to national stability.

books.title: The Fourth Turning Is Here
books.summary: "The Fourth Turning is Here" builds upon Neil Howe's previous book, the Fourth Turning that he wrote along with his co-author [--]. The books argue that history moves in predictable 80-100 year cycles comprised of four distinct generational turnings, with each cycle culminating in a crisis period that fundamentally reshapes society. In this book he contends that America has entered the 'Fourth Turning', a critical historical phase characterized by institutional upheaval, economic distress, and social transformation. He explains how current events, including the COVID-19 pandemic, political polarization, technological disruption, and economic instability, align with previous Fourth Turnings and on the basis of that contends that the crisis period that began around 2008 will likely intensify through the 2020s. The book's central message is that while these crisis periods are challenging and potentially dangerous, they are also necessary for societal renewal, and understanding this pattern can help us navigate through the turbulent times ahead and potentially emerge stronger on the other side.

books.title: The Fourth Turning
books.summary: A theory of history as a recurring cycle of four generational “turnings” that repeat every 80–100 years: the High, Awakening, Unraveling, and Crisis. Each turning reflects the interaction of four archetypal generations—Prophets, Nomads, Heroes, and Artists—whose attitudes and behaviors shape society’s trajectory. The authors argue that the United States was entering a Fourth Turning (a Crisis era) in the early 2000s, akin to previous periods such as the American Revolution, Civil War, and Great Depression/World War II. They predict that this Crisis would fundamentally transform American institutions and values, creating both great danger and an opportunity for national renewal, depending on how society responds.

books.title: The Future of Humanity
books.summary: Humanity’s long-term prospects depend on it becoming a multi-planetary species. Kaku surveys current advances in space travel, terraforming, robotics, AI, and biotechnology, linking them to possibilities of colonising Mars, mining asteroids, and exploring exoplanets. He discusses scientific hurdles—radiation, interstellar distances, resource constraints—as well as ethical and political questions about expansion beyond Earth. Drawing parallels with earlier human migrations and technological revolutions, Kaku concludes that while challenges are immense, the trajectory of science makes space colonisation and eventual interstellar travel plausible, positioning humanity to outlast planetary threats and evolve into a cosmic civilisation.

books.title: The Future of Ideas
books.summary: The Future of Ideas argues that the internet’s explosive creativity came from its unique architecture: a blend of open commons (such as code, protocols, and ideas) and limited private control that allowed free exchange, innovation, and remixing. Lessig warns that this balance is being eroded by expanding intellectual property rights, restrictive licensing, and corporate control of infrastructure, which threaten to choke the openness that made digital innovation possible. Through historical examples and legal analysis, he shows how enclosure of the information commons stifles cultural and technological progress, and calls for policies that preserve openness as the foundation for continued creativity and growth.

books.title: The Gated Republic
books.summary: India’s democracy has increasingly failed to deliver basic public goods—such as education, healthcare, housing, water, and security—pushing citizens to seek private, “gated” solutions. Through case studies across sectors, Aiyar shows how the state’s inability to provide reliable services has created parallel systems: private schools, private hospitals, gated communities, water tankers, and private security, accessible mainly to those who can pay. This withdrawal of the state from core responsibilities has widened inequality and undermined the social contract, leaving the poor dependent on a dysfunctional public system while the middle and upper classes exit into privatized enclaves. The book concludes that without systemic reform and accountable governance, India risks deepening segregation between those inside and outside these “gates.”

books.title: The Gene
books.summary: The history, science, and ethical dilemmas of genetics, from Gregor Mendel’s pea plant experiments and Darwin’s theory of evolution to the discovery of DNA’s structure and the rise of modern genomics. Mukherjee weaves together scientific milestones with personal narratives, including his own family’s struggles with hereditary mental illness, to show how genes shape identity, health, and destiny. The book explores both the promises of genetic research—curing diseases, personalized medicine, gene editing—and its dangers, such as eugenics, discrimination, and the temptation to engineer human traits. Mukherjee concludes that while the gene is one of the most powerful concepts in science, its manipulation demands humility, caution, and ethical foresight.

books.title: The Golden Road
books.summary: A book about how the Golden Road to India predated the Silk Road to China.

books.title: The Great Arc
books.summary: The story of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, the audacious nineteenth-century project to measure the subcontinent along a meridian arc from the southern tip to the Himalayas. Keay recounts the decades of labor, disease, and obsessive precision led by William Lambton and George Everest, a feat of scientific endurance that mapped India and incidentally measured the world's highest mountain.

books.title: The Great Tech Game
books.summary: Global competition in the 21st century is a struggle for technological supremacy, and nations’ economic growth, geopolitical influence, and social stability increasingly hinge on how well they play this “game.” Suri outlines four levels of the contest—semiconductors and hardware, software and platforms, data and networks, and artificial intelligence—showing how each builds on the other to create compounding advantages. He emphasises that technology is not just about innovation but about ecosystems: policy, talent, capital, and institutions that allow breakthroughs to scale. Using comparisons across the U.S., China, India, and other countries, Suri warns that nations failing to invest and strategise will fall behind irreversibly. The book concludes with prescriptions for how India can position itself to compete, stressing digital infrastructure, skills, and regulatory foresight.

books.title: The Greatest Invention
books.summary:
A fascinating journey through the origins and evolution of writing, one of humanity's most transformative achievements. Ferrara explores how writing systems developed independently in various parts of the world, including Mesopotamia, Egypt, China, Meso-America, and beyond.*

*Ferrara examines nine enigmatic scripts that represent different stages and styles of writing, many of which remain undeciphered or only partially understood. These include the iconic cuneiform, the intricate hieroglyphs, and mysterious scripts such as Rongorongo from Easter Island and the undeciphered Linear A.*

*Ferrara delves into the creative sparks that led to these systems, arguing that writing was not an inevitable byproduct of human development but rather a remarkable invention born from human ingenuity. She celebrates the diversity of these scripts, emphasizing their significance in shaping cultures, religions, economies, and histories.*

*By blending archaeology, linguistics, and cultural history, Ferrara weaves a narrative that highlights the deep connection between writing and the human drive to communicate, record, and express ideas. She also explores the ongoing mysteries surrounding undeciphered scripts, inspiring a sense of wonder and curiosity about the past.

books.title: The Grid
books.summary: The Grid unpacks the sprawling, aging electrical infrastructure of the United States—an often invisible yet crucial machine powering modern life. Bakke takes readers from the fragmented local grids of Edison’s time through the consolidation into regional systems, and the rise of monopolistic utilities dominated by figures like Samuel Insull. She explores how cascading blackouts (like the Northeast blackout of 2003) reveal systemic fragility rooted in outdated design, misaligned incentives, and regulatory inertia. As green energy and digital expectations mount, the grid confronts new pressures: integrating intermittent renewables, managing peak demand, enabling distributed generation, and deploying smart technology—all while safeguarding reliability and public trust. Bakke argues that the grid must be fundamentally reimagined—moving from a centralized, brittle web into a resilient, decentralized, future-proof ecosystem.

books.title: The Gujaratis
books.summary: The Gujaratis is a sweeping and deeply researched portrait of the Gujarati community in all its diversity—covering those who live in Gujarat and those in the large diaspora. Over 12 parts and 80-odd chapters, it explores history, language, caste, religion, politics, commerce, art, literature, food, family, identity, and migration. Tripathi uses interviews, archival sources, his own memories, and on-the-ground reporting to show both the strengths (enterprise, adaptability, cultural pride) and the tensions (caste hierarchies, communal strife, inequalities, contradictions) that define Gujarati life. He looks into how Gujaratis abroad maintain identity, how dialects and cultural practices vary within Gujarat, how “Gujarati-ness” is felt and invoked in politics and popular culture, and how myth and idealization coexist with critique and self-reflection.

books.title: The Half-Life of Facts
books.summary: Knowledge evolves, and facts are not fixed but decay, change, or are replaced over time in predictable patterns. Drawing on research in scientometrics and the sociology of knowledge, Arbesman demonstrates that scientific and social “truths” have measurable rates of obsolescence, much like radioactive half-lives. He illustrates this with examples ranging from medicine and astronomy to everyday facts, revealing how what we “know” today may be overturned tomorrow. The book argues that instead of clinging to permanence, we should embrace the provisional nature of knowledge, cultivate scientific literacy, and build systems that adapt to continual change.

books.title: The Hidden Half
books.summary: The Hidden Half explores the vast role of uncertainty, chance, and unknown factors in shaping outcomes in science, medicine, economics, and everyday life. Blastland argues that despite advances in data and predictive models, a large portion of causality remains hidden—what he calls the “hidden half”—leading to unexpected variations and failures in our understanding. Through examples ranging from clinical trials and genetics to social behaviour and economic policy, he shows how identical inputs can produce radically different results, challenging the assumption that human systems are fully knowable or controllable. The book concludes that humility about what we cannot explain is essential, and that embracing uncertainty can lead to better science, policy, and decision-making.

books.title: The Hidden Life of Trees
books.summary: The Hidden Life of Trees by Peter Wohlleben explores the remarkable and often unseen ways in which trees communicate, cooperate, and thrive in forest ecosystems. Drawing on scientific research and his own experiences as a forester in Germany, Wohlleben presents trees not as passive organisms, but as social beings with networks akin to communities. He describes how trees use underground fungal networks—sometimes called the “Wood Wide Web”—to share nutrients, warn each other of danger, and support sick or young trees. The book emphasises the importance of companionship among trees, showing that they grow best in groups and can even exhibit signs of memory and learning. Wohlleben’s writing challenges the traditional view of plants as inert life forms, encouraging readers to see forests as vibrant, interconnected systems with intelligence and sensitivity. He argues that modern forestry practices often ignore these complex dynamics, damaging long-term forest health. Blending poetic storytelling with ecological science, The Hidden Life of Trees calls for a deeper respect for nature and urges a reconsideration of how humans manage and relate to forests. Ultimately, the book is a passionate plea for conservation, highlighting the hidden wonders of the natural world just beneath our feet.

books.title: The Idea Factory
books.summary: The story of Bell Labs, the legendary research institution that produced many of the 20th century’s most important innovations, including the transistor, the laser, information theory, and the foundations of the digital age. Gertner traces how the unique structure of Bell Labs—its mix of scientists, engineers, and visionaries working under one roof with long-term funding from AT&T’s monopoly profits—created a model for collaborative innovation. The book profiles key figures like Claude Shannon, William Shockley, and Mervin Kelly, showing how their discoveries transformed technology, business, and society. It also examines why such an institution is difficult to replicate today, as corporate research has shifted toward short-term returns.

books.title: The Identity Project
books.summary: The Identity Project investigates how India’s democracy has been undermined through a mix of political, social, and technological strategies. Bhatia opens with the 2020 Delhi riots and the struggles of victims like Nisar, then traces the roots of growing sectarian division through historical movements from the 1800s and 20th‑century Hindu nationalist organisations. He connects this to contemporary shifts—such as the CAA-NRC debates, the rise of Aadhaar, state surveillance, and disinformation campaigns—and shows how governance has been captured by ideological and sectarian forces. Through detailed reportage, personal stories, and archival research, the book chronicles how communal identity has been weaponised, democratic norms eroded, and ordinary citizens left in the crossfire—painting a vivid, unsettling picture of modern India’s political trajectory.

books.title: The Incarcerations
books.summary: An investigation into the Bhima Koregaon case, in which sixteen intellectuals, lawyers, and activists—the "BK-16"—were imprisoned under anti-terror laws on charges Shah scrutinizes as fabricated, including evidence apparently planted on their computers. Anthropologist Alpa Shah tells the story of these prisoners of conscience as a window onto the erosion of democracy, civil liberties, and dissent in contemporary India.

books.title: The Indian Conservative
books.summary: A survey of Indian right-wing thought that reframes conservatism not as reactionary politics but as a coherent philosophy favouring gradual change, respect for tradition, individual liberty, and a minimalist state. Rao, the entrepreneur who founded Mphasis, traces conservative strands across five domains—economics, politics, culture, society, and aesthetics—and argues that their roots run deep in Indian texts like the Shanti Parva and the Tirukkural, long predating Burke or Scruton.

books.title: The Inevitable
books.summary: There are twelve technological forces—such as becoming, cognifying, flowing, screening, accessing, sharing, filtering, remixing, tracking, and questioning—that will inevitably shape the future. Kelly contends that these trends are not optional but built into the logic of technological progress, and resisting them is futile; the real challenge is to understand and guide their impact. He illustrates how advances in AI, virtual reality, the sharing economy, and constant connectivity will transform work, culture, and daily life, emphasising adaptation over control. The book concludes that embracing these forces with foresight and creativity will allow societies and individuals to thrive in a rapidly changing technological environment.

books.title: The Infinity Machine
books.summary: An account of the past fifteen years of artificial intelligence told largely through Demis Hassabis, the chess prodigy and neuroscientist who founded DeepMind. Drawing on more than thirty hours with Hassabis as well as his rivals and critics, Mallaby chronicles the breakthroughs (including the protein-folding triumph of AlphaFold), the struggles over AI safety, and the fierce competition with OpenAI in the race toward superintelligence.

books.title: The Innovator's Dilemma
books.summary: The Innovator’s Dilemma explains why well-managed, successful companies often fail when confronted with disruptive innovations. Christensen distinguishes between **sustaining innovations**—improvements that serve existing customers with better performance—and **disruptive innovations**—simpler, cheaper, initially lower-performing technologies that appeal to new or underserved markets. Because established firms focus on satisfying their most profitable customers, they ignore these early-stage disruptors, allowing smaller entrants to improve them until they overtake incumbents. Through case studies like disk drives, excavators, and retailing, Christensen shows that the very practices that make companies successful—listening to customers, focusing on profits, and improving existing products—also blind them to transformative change.

books.title: The Innovators
books.summary: The Innovators traces the collaborative, evolving journey of the digital revolution—from Ada Lovelace’s conceptual groundwork for programmable machines to the rise of the internet and modern computing. Walter Isaacson profiles a vast cast of contributors—including Ada Lovelace, Alan Turing, Grace Hopper, the creators of the transistor, early microchip innovators, video game pioneers, the architects of the Internet and the Web, and startup icons—showing how each breakthrough emerged through interplay among creative individuals, engineers, governments, academia, and entrepreneurial ecosystems. The narrative emphasizes innovation as a cumulative, networked process—fuelled by serendipitous meetings and shared purpose—not the feat of lone geniuses.

books.title: The Internationalists
books.summary: A single event—the signing of the 1928 Kellogg-Briand Pact, which outlawed war as a tool of national policy—fundamentally reshaped the international order. While initially dismissed as naïve, the pact marked a turning point: before it, conquest was a legitimate means of acquiring territory, but afterwards, aggressive war became delegitimised and increasingly punished. They trace how this shift, reinforced by World War II and institutions like the United Nations, fostered a decline in interstate wars of conquest and enabled the modern system of global trade and cooperation. The book concludes that although wars still occur, the legal and normative transformation set in motion by the pact continues to shape world politics.

books.title: The Invention of Science
books.summary: The Scientific Revolution of the 16th and 17th centuries was not just a collection of discoveries but the birth of a new way of thinking that fundamentally transformed human understanding of the world. Wootton shows how innovations—from the telescope and microscope to the printing press—combined with new concepts like evidence, fact, and experiment to create modern science as a distinct enterprise. He emphasizes the shift in language and thought, as terms such as “discovery,” “theory,” and “laws of nature” acquired their modern meanings, enabling a break from Aristotelian and scholastic traditions. The book concludes that this intellectual revolution was as significant as the invention of democracy or capitalism in shaping the modern world.

books.title: The Journalist and the Murderer
books.summary: The Journalist and the Murderer examines the fraught ethics of journalism through the case of Jeffrey MacDonald, a convicted murderer, and Joe McGinniss, the journalist who wrote Fatal Vision about him. Malcolm dissects how McGinniss gained MacDonald’s trust by presenting himself as sympathetic, only to later portray him as guilty, raising questions about betrayal, truth-telling, and the moral compromises inherent in the journalist–subject relationship. She argues that journalism is an inherently “morally indefensible” profession because it requires extracting stories from subjects who may not fully understand how they will be represented. Using the MacDonald–McGinniss case as a lens, Malcolm explores the blurred boundaries between fact, narrative, and manipulation.

books.title: The Last Pirate of New York
books.summary: The true story of Albert W. Hicks, a 19th-century criminal who became the last man executed for piracy in New York in 1860. Cohen reconstructs Hicks’s life of crime—burglary, robbery, and ultimately the brutal murder of three men aboard a ship near Staten Island—and shows how his trial and execution captured the public imagination in an era fascinated by crime and sensational journalism. Hicks became a dark folk hero, embodying both fear and fascination with lawlessness at a time when New York was rapidly transforming into a modern metropolis.

books.title: The Life and Times of George Fernandes
books.summary: A comprehensive biography of the Indian trade unionist, socialist leader, and politician who rose from humble beginnings to become a central figure in Indian public life. The book traces Fernandes’s early struggles as a labour organiser in Mumbai, his role in building powerful unions, and his transformation into a fiery opposition leader against Indira Gandhi during the Emergency. It explores his maverick political career—his tenure as a minister in multiple governments, his controversial decisions, such as during the Kargil War as Defence Minister, and his complex ideological journey from socialism to alliances with the BJP. Ramagundam situates Fernandes within the broader shifts of Indian politics, from socialist movements and coalition governments to the rise of Hindutva, presenting him as both an icon of dissent and a symbol of contradictions.

books.title: The Making of Aadhaar
books.summary: An insider’s account of how India built the world’s largest biometric identification system. As the first Director General of the Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI), Sharma recounts the project’s conceptualization, the technological and administrative challenges of enrolling over a billion people, and the institutional innovations that made it possible. The book details how Aadhaar was designed as a foundational ID to enable access to welfare schemes, financial services, and digital infrastructure, while also addressing concerns of security, scalability, and inclusion. Sharma emphasizes the collaborative effort between government, technologists, and private partners, presenting Aadhaar as a model of large-scale digital public infrastructure.

books.title: The Man From the Future
books.summary: A biography of John von Neumann, the Hungarian-American polymath whose work laid the foundations for modern computing, game theory, nuclear strategy, and much of today’s digital world. The book traces his early brilliance in mathematics, his contributions to the Manhattan Project, and his pivotal role in designing the architecture that underpins nearly all computers. Bhattacharya shows how von Neumann’s ideas—on self-replicating systems, artificial intelligence, and the mathematics of conflict and cooperation—anticipated technologies and dilemmas that still shape the 21st century. The narrative presents him as both a product of his time and a visionary whose insights continue to influence science, economics, and geopolitics.

books.title: The Man of Numbers
books.summary: A biography of Leonardo of Pisa, better known as Fibonacci, the medieval mathematician who introduced Hindu–Arabic numerals and arithmetic to Europe through his 1202 book Liber Abaci. Devlin explains how Fibonacci’s advocacy of the numeral system—using digits 0–9 and place value—replaced cumbersome Roman numerals and revolutionised trade, finance, and science in Europe. The book also explores the famous Fibonacci sequence, though noting it was a minor part of his work compared to his transformative impact on practical mathematics. Devlin situates Fibonacci within the broader cultural exchange between the Arab world and Europe, showing how his contributions helped lay the groundwork for the Renaissance and modern mathematics.

books.title: The Meaning of It All
books.summary: A slim volume gathering three public lectures Feynman delivered in 1963 on the relationship between science and society. With characteristic candour he reflects on the uncertainty at the heart of scientific thinking, the uneasy coexistence of science and religion, and the responsibilities and irrationalities of a democratic culture grappling with knowledge and doubt.

books.title: The Moral Case for Fossil Fuels
books.summary: Despite environmental concerns, fossil fuels have been overwhelmingly beneficial to humanity by powering industrial civilization, lifting billions out of poverty, and extending life expectancy. Epstein contends that mainstream discussions focus too narrowly on the negative impacts of fossil fuels—such as climate change—while neglecting their role in providing reliable, affordable energy that enables food production, medical advances, and economic growth. He challenges prevailing climate models and argues that human adaptability, aided by technology and energy abundance, mitigates environmental risks.

books.title: The Network State
books.summary: The Network State by Balaji Srinivasan lays out a vision for how online communities can evolve into full-fledged, sovereign entities—what he calls “network states.” He argues that the internet enables people to coordinate globally around shared values, form digital-first communities with collective identity, and then leverage their scale and cohesion to negotiate recognition, territory, and influence in the physical world. Srinivasan contrasts this with traditional nation-states, which are geographically bound, and suggests that cloud-based organization allows for voluntary societies that transcend borders. The book explores practical aspects of founding such states, including fundraising through crypto, building parallel economies, developing social contracts, and seeking diplomatic legitimacy. Ultimately, it proposes that network states could solve governance failures by allowing people to “opt in” to systems that better reflect their beliefs, thus creating competition among forms of government.

books.title: The Network
books.summary: The Network by Scott Woolley tells the story of the invention, commercialisation, and regulation of radio in the United States, focusing on the battle between RCA/NBC and AT&T in the 1920s and 1930s over who would control the new medium of broadcasting. Woolley shows how David Sarnoff at RCA pushed for a national broadcasting system that would bring radio into every home, while AT&T initially tried to dominate radio by charging for “toll broadcasting,” treating stations like telephone lines. The book details the technological innovations, patent fights, and government interventions that determined which model would prevail, ultimately leading to NBC’s rise as the first national radio network. Woolley uses this conflict to illustrate how business strategies, regulation, and public interest considerations shaped not only the radio industry but also the broader media landscape of the twentieth century.

books.title: The Order of Time
books.summary: The Order of Time explores the nature of time as understood by modern physics, showing how our intuitive sense of a universal, flowing time dissolves under scientific scrutiny. Rovelli explains that time does not exist as a single, absolute entity: relativity demonstrates that it flows differently depending on speed and gravity, while quantum theory suggests time emerges from interactions rather than existing independently. He dismantles concepts such as the present moment, the arrow of time, and linear causality, arguing that they are approximations rooted in human perception and thermodynamics rather than fundamental truths. In the final part, Rovelli reflects on how to live meaningfully in a universe without absolute time, emphasising memory, relationships, and experience as the anchors of human existence.

books.title: The People vs Tech
books.summary: The People vs Tech examines how digital technologies—from social media platforms to big data and AI—are undermining the foundations of liberal democracy. Bartlett argues that democracy depends on informed citizens, shared truths, individual autonomy, and fair institutions, but each of these pillars is being eroded: algorithms polarise debate, surveillance capitalism compromises privacy, targeted propaganda manipulates voters, and automation threatens economic stability. Drawing on global political trends, he shows how populists and authoritarians exploit these dynamics, while democratic institutions struggle to adapt. Bartlett concludes that unless democracies rapidly reform—through stronger regulation of tech companies, new norms around data use, and renewed civic engagement—technological power will tilt societies toward authoritarianism.

books.title: The Politics of Innovation
books.summary: An examination of why some nations become leaders in science and technology while others lag. Synthesizing decades of research, Taylor argues that the usual "five pillars"—property rights, R&D funding, education, research universities, and trade—cannot fully explain innovation rates, and proposes instead that external threats and internal rivalries shape whether a country can muster the political will to innovate.

books.title: The Politics of Time
books.summary: The Politics of Time argues that time has always been politically controlled by those in power. Standing traces how ancient Greeks distinguished between labour (paid, onerous work), self-chosen work, recreation, leisure, and contemplation (schole)—a distinction largely lost today. Since the industrial era, capitalism has homogenised time, turning jobs into the central meaning of life while rendering unpaid but essential work like caregiving invisible. In our current "tertiary time" regime, precarious workers experience stolen time amid chronic uncertainty and rising mental health struggles. Standing calls instead for a “politics of time” that reclaims time for meaningful activity—including care, civic engagement, commoning, and purposeful leisure—offering a framework for social emancipation and ecological sustainability.

books.title: The Premonition
books.summary: The story of how a small group of American doctors, scientists, and public health officials recognised the grave threat of pandemics long before COVID-19, but whose warnings were largely ignored by the U.S. government. Lewis focuses on figures like Charity Dean, Carter Mecher, and other unconventional thinkers who developed strategies for pandemic preparedness, including social distancing and early intervention, based on lessons from past outbreaks. He contrasts their foresight and urgency with the bureaucratic inertia, political dysfunction, and institutional failures of agencies like the CDC, showing how systemic reluctance to act decisively allowed the coronavirus to spread unchecked. The book highlights how individual initiative and maverick thinking often outpace official channels in times of crisis.

books.title: The Privacy Fallacy
books.summary:
The McGill law professor starts from an unsettling premise: contemporary privacy law is built on ideas invented for an analogue world and bent around market logic. Those ideas—chief among them the belief that individuals can rationally “trade” personal data for services—have trapped regulators in a notice‑and‑consent cul‑de‑sac while tech firms refine the art of extraction. 

Cofone devotes the first half of the book to dismantling what he calls privacy’s “zombie myths.” He punctures the so‑called _privacy paradox_ (the claim that people say they value privacy yet give it away), the “nothing‑to‑hide” cliché, and the assumption that disclosure decisions are fully informed and freely chosen. Behavioural research, he shows, reveals a public navigating uncertainty, dark‑pattern design and power asymmetries—not apathy. This myth‑busting sets the stage for a wider critique: if the law keeps treating privacy as an individual preference, it will never address the systemic harms baked into data‑driven economies.

Those harms, Cofone argues, are less about hurt feelings or stolen identities than about **manipulation, discrimination and unequal bargaining power**. Algorithmic credit scoring, predictive policing and targeted advertising all translate personal data into levers that entrench existing inequities. Yet current rules—modelled on contract and property doctrines—recognise only economic losses or security breaches, leaving the most pervasive injuries legally invisible.

The final chapters outline a corrective: a **new liability regime that shifts accountability from users to data‑controllers**. Cofone proposes treating privacy wrongs as tort‑like “power harms,” imposing duty‑of‑care obligations on firms that profit from personal information. He sketches practical reforms—strict liability for certain AI inferences, bans on anti‑privacy design, collective redress for group‑level discrimination—while warning that half‑measures will merely entrench the status quo. The book closes on a call for lawmakers to abandon the comforting fiction that privacy can be individually negotiated and to confront the structural power dynamics at the heart of the information economy. It is a concise, accessible brief that should unsettle technologists, regulators and anyone still hoping to click their way to safety online.

books.title: The Private Is Political
books.summary: The Private Is Political argues that privacy in the digital age is not an individual preference to be managed with settings but a structural, relational condition shaped by platforms, data brokers, and social inequalities. Alice E. Marwick shows how “networked privacy” operates across feeds, algorithms, and data markets to expose people—especially women, LGBTQ+ users, racialized communities, and the poor—to harassment, doxing, non-consensual sharing, and reputational harm, even when they personally act cautiously. Through interviews and case studies, she explains concepts like context collapse, privacy labor (the ongoing work users perform to protect themselves), and the “violation machine” that turns intimate traces into profit and control; she situates these harms in broader economies of surveillance and attention; and she ends by urging legal, platform, and cultural reforms that treat privacy as a collective right requiring accountability from powerful intermediaries rather than more burden on individuals.

books.title: The Prize
books.summary: "The Prize" presents a comprehensive history of the global oil industry, arguing that petroleum has been the pivotal commodity shaping world politics, power, and economic development since the late 19th century. It demonstrates how oil has been at the center of the most significant [[geopolitical]] events of the modern era - from both World Wars to the rise of Middle Eastern politics, from the formation of global energy markets to the emergence of national oil companies and international corporations. The book's unifying message is that understanding the history of oil is essential to understanding modern civilization itself, as the pursuit, control, and exploitation of this vital resource has not only fueled economic growth and technological progress but has also consistently determined the rise and fall of nations, shaped international relations, and continues to be the crucial factor in global power dynamics, energy security, and the future of human development.

books.title: The Progressive Maharaja
books.summary:
A book that is essentially a reproduction of Sir Madhava Rao’s _Hints on the Art and Science of Government_ - a long-overlooked guide to governance, offering advice on statecraft, administration, and public policy. Written in English during the colonial era, the treatise reflects Rao’s deep engagement with both Indian and Western traditions of political thought. It addresses critical topics such as the ethical responsibilities of rulers, economic development, justice, education, and the management of public resources.

Rahul Sagar contextualizes the historical significance of Rao’s work in the introductory essay illustrating how Rao’s pragmatic and progressive approach laid a foundation for modern Indian governance, blending traditional Indian values with the necessities of modernization during a time of colonial domination.

This scholarly yet accessible work serves as a testament to the intellectual legacy of Sir Madhava Rao and invites readers to appreciate the nuanced debates on governance that shaped India’s political awakening. It appeals to historians, political scientists, and anyone interested in the roots of modern governance in South Asia.

books.title: The Prosperity Paradox
books.summary: The book challenges the conventional approaches to economic development, arguing that prosperity in poor nations is not driven primarily by foreign aid or infrastructure investment but by “market-creating innovations.” These are products and services that make something previously inaccessible affordable and accessible to a mass market, thereby creating jobs, building infrastructure, and fostering self-sustaining growth. Using case studies from around the world, the authors show how companies that solved for affordability and accessibility transformed entire economies, often doing more than governments or NGOs to lift people out of poverty. They argue that aid too often treats symptoms rather than causes, while innovation stimulates demand that pulls resources, institutions, and capital into place.

books.title: The Psychology of Money
books.summary: The Psychology of Money explores how people’s attitudes, biases, and behaviours toward money often matter more than financial knowledge or technical skill. Through short stories and examples, Housel shows that wealth is less about income or investment returns and more about habits like patience, saving, and risk management. He emphasises the role of luck and timing, the dangers of envy and comparison, and the importance of defining “enough.” The book also explains why compounding works best with long time horizons, why personal finance is deeply emotional, and why financial decisions should be tailored to individual goals rather than abstract models. Housel concludes that humility, frugality, and long-term consistency are the true foundations of financial success.

books.title: The Rule of Laws
books.summary: A sweeping four-thousand-year history of law across civilizations, from ancient Mesopotamia and India to China, Rome, the Islamic world, and the modern West. Pirie, an Oxford legal anthropologist, shows how law has served both to bind rulers and to entrench their power, and argues for its enduring role as humanity's most sophisticated tool for creating order and constraining tyranny.

books.title: The Science of Star Wars
books.summary: The Science of Star Wars examines the technologies, phenomena, and creatures depicted in the Star Wars universe through the lens of real-world science. The book analyses whether lightsabers, droids, faster-than-light travel, the Force, and alien life forms could exist within the laws of physics, biology, and engineering as we know them. Cavelos draws on astrophysics, robotics, genetics, and neuroscience to explore what is theoretically possible, what is speculative, and what firmly belongs in science fiction. By separating fact from fantasy, she shows how Star Wars reflects humanity’s scientific aspirations and limitations, while also inspiring innovation.

books.title: The Seventh Sense
books.summary: The Seventh Sense argues that the defining skill of the modern age is the ability to understand and harness networks—digital, financial, political, and social—that now govern power and change in the world. Ramo explains that traditional institutions and hierarchies are being destabilised by hyperconnectivity, where influence comes from controlling the flow of connections rather than holding fixed assets. He explores how this shift empowers new actors, from tech companies to terrorists, and makes the world more volatile and unpredictable. The “seventh sense” is the instinct to see the patterns of networks, anticipate how they evolve, and act effectively within them. He concludes that mastering this sense will determine which nations, organisations, and individuals thrive in the networked era.

books.title: The Spider Network
books.summary: The Spider Network tells the inside story of the LIBOR scandal, in which a group of traders and bankers manipulated the world’s most important interest rate for profit. Focusing on Tom Hayes, a brilliant but socially awkward trader at UBS and Citigroup, the book shows how he built a network of brokers and colleagues across major banks to nudge LIBOR submissions in directions that benefited their positions. Enrich traces how this manipulation went unchecked for years, aided by a culture of greed, lax oversight, and widespread complicity within the financial industry. The narrative also follows the eventual investigations and prosecutions that exposed the scandal, with Hayes cast as both mastermind and scapegoat.

books.title: The Square and the Tower
books.summary: The Square and the Tower examines the tension between hierarchical structures (“the tower”) and networks of individuals (“the square”) in shaping history. Ferguson argues that while hierarchies like states, churches, and corporations have traditionally dominated, informal networks—such as secret societies, revolutionary groups, or online platforms—have often been the real drivers of change. He traces this dynamic from the Renaissance and the Enlightenment through the world wars and the Cold War, up to the digital age, showing how networks can disrupt established orders but also struggle to sustain stability. The book concludes that in today’s hyperconnected world, understanding the interplay between networks and hierarchies is essential to making sense of political upheaval, populism, and the future of global order.

books.title: The Struggle and the Promise
books.summary: A wide-ranging diagnosis of what holds India back and what could unlock its potential, written by the industrialist co-chairman of Forbes Marshall. Across chapters on policy, industry, higher education, research, and institutions, Forbes argues for getting the balance right between the state and private enterprise, and lays out an actionable blueprint for building an innovative, more prosperous country.

books.title: The Tech Coup
books.summary: An argument that private technology companies have quietly usurped powers that once belonged to states—over speech, surveillance, security, and even foreign policy—hollowing out democratic governance. Drawing on her experience as a European parliamentarian, Schaake charts how this shift happened and proposes concrete measures to reassert public and democratic control over the tech sector.

books.title: The Third Pillar
books.summary: The Third Pillar argues that society is supported by three pillars—the state, the market, and the community—and that modern crises stem from the neglect of the third pillar. Rajan shows how globalisation and technological change have strengthened markets and states while hollowing out local communities, leading to inequality, political polarisation, and social discontent. He traces the historical balance between the three pillars, from early agrarian societies through industrialisation to the digital age, highlighting how community institutions once mediated between government and business. Rajan calls for a rebalancing, where policies empower local communities, decentralise decision-making, and restore the social fabric without abandoning the benefits of global markets and strong states.

books.title: The Truth Machine
books.summary: The Truth Machine examines the transformative potential of blockchain technology, arguing that it represents a new architecture of trust in a world where traditional institutions—banks, governments, and corporations—have repeatedly failed to uphold it. The book traces the history of money, finance, and recordkeeping to show how centralised intermediaries came to dominate trust systems, and then explains how blockchain’s decentralised, immutable ledgers could displace these intermediaries by allowing individuals to transact directly and verifiably. Through examples across finance, supply chains, identity management, and governance, the authors highlight both the opportunities (efficiency, transparency, democratisation) and challenges (scalability, regulation, misuse) of blockchain adoption. Ultimately, they argue that while blockchain will not eliminate institutions altogether, it will force them to evolve into more accountable and transparent actors within a new trust framework.

books.title: The Truths and Lies of Nationalism as Narrated by Charvak
books.summary: An interesting book that uses the skeptical, materialist voice of the ancient philosopher Charvak to interrogate India’s contemporary nationalism—separating the emotional “truths” of belonging, pride and civilizational memory from the “lies” that recast a Hindu majoritarian project as nation-building. The book traces how historical revisionism, culture-war rhetoric, and centralised power reframe citizenship and dissent, while data on jobs, growth, welfare and inequality undercut triumphalist claims of economic renaissance. It distinguishes civic, constitutional patriotism from ethnoreligious identity politics; examines the stress placed on institutions, minorities and federalism by propaganda, surveillance and polarisation; and argues that myth-laden narratives distract from governance failures. It concludes by urging a return to rational inquiry, pluralism, and constitutional checks as the only durable basis for national solidarity.

books.title: The Twenty-Six Words That Created the Internet
books.summary: The Twenty-Six Words That Created the Internet examines Section 230 of the U.S. Communications Decency Act—those “twenty-six words” that grant online platforms immunity from liability for user-generated content—and how this short legal clause became the foundation of the modern internet. Kosseff traces its origins in the 1990s debates over online moderation, explaining how it enabled platforms like Google, Facebook, Twitter, and Wikipedia to host vast amounts of speech without constant litigation. Through legal cases and policy battles, he shows how Section 230 balanced free expression with moderation, fostering innovation while also shielding companies from responsibility for harms such as misinformation and harassment. The book concludes by arguing that while Section 230 was vital to the internet’s growth, its unintended consequences now pose hard questions about accountability, regulation, and the future of online discourse.

books.title: The Tyranny of Merit
books.summary: A critique of meritocracy as a governing ideal, arguing that the belief that success is earned and deserved breeds hubris among winners and humiliation among those left behind. Sandel traces how the "rhetoric of rising" corroded the dignity of work and fuelled populist backlash, and calls for a politics of the common good that values contribution over credentialed achievement.

books.title: The Tyranny of Metrics
books.summary: The Tyranny of Metrics argues that the drive to measure performance with standardized indicators—test scores, targets, rankings, KPIs—often distorts behavior, crowds out judgment, and degrades the very outcomes it seeks to improve. Drawing examples from education, medicine, policing, the military, business, and philanthropy, Jerry Z. Muller shows how metric fixation induces gaming, teaching to the test, data falsification, risk aversion, and mission drift; ignores context and professional expertise; and conflates what’s measurable with what matters. He explains why incentives tied to metrics magnify these pathologies (Goodhart’s Law) and why transparency and accountability regimes frequently backfire when they substitute numbers for trust. The book concludes by proposing a more modest, pluralistic approach: use measurement as a tool—diagnostic, not punitive—selected and interpreted by domain experts, complemented by qualitative assessment, and bounded by clear awareness of costs, incentives, and unintended consequences.

books.title: The Victorian Internet
books.summary: The Victorian Internet recounts how the 19th-century electric telegraph created the first global communications network and unleashed many of the same phenomena later associated with the internet: real-time long-distance conversation, new professions and subcultures of operators, cross-border business and finance, hype cycles and utopian claims, along with frauds, privacy breaches, “hacking,” romance across wires, and regulatory debates over standards and monopoly control. Tom Standage traces the system’s rapid build-out, the technical and organisational innovations (codes, relays, time-keeping, undersea cables) that made it scale, and the ways it compressed distance, reordered journalism and markets, and fostered both cooperation and conflict among nations and corporations, before being normalised—and partly eclipsed—by the telephone. His conclusion is that communication revolutions follow recurring patterns: transformative early promises, disruptive social effects, predictable misuses, and eventual institutional accommodation.

books.title: The Wealth of Humans
books.summary: The Wealth of Humans_ argues that digital technologies and globalization have made human labor abundant, eroding workers’ bargaining power and pushing a growing share of value toward scarce assets—urban agglomerations, intellectual property, platforms, and the social capital embedded in elite networks and institutions. Ryan Avent traces how automation thins middle-skill jobs, credentialism and licensing gatekeep opportunity, superstar firms and expensive cities concentrate rents, and frayed social contracts fuel political backlash; he emphasizes that prosperity now depends less on individual effort than on access to productive ecosystems. The book’s policy program focuses on shifting and sharing rents by loosening housing constraints in productive cities, reforming IP and occupational licensing, encouraging migration and firm entry, investing in skills and experimentation, strengthening social insurance (up to and including income supports), and rebuilding institutions that enable cooperation and wage growth. His conclusion is that without deliberate redistribution of the new scarcities and renewal of civic and workplace institutions, technological progress will keep widening inequality and undermining democratic stability.

books.title: The Wizard and the Prophet
books.summary: The Wizard and the Prophet contrasts two archetypal approaches to humanity’s future through the lives of Norman Borlaug (the “Wizard”) and William Vogt (the “Prophet”). Borlaug, the Green Revolution agronomist, believed in using science, technology, and innovation to expand Earth’s carrying capacity and solve problems of scarcity. Vogt, the pioneering ecologist, argued that human survival depends on restraint, balance with nature, and limits to growth. Mann uses their opposing philosophies to frame contemporary debates on climate change, food, water, and energy—between technological optimism and ecological realism. Tracing their intellectual legacies through modern policy, agriculture, and environmentalism, the book concludes that our future will hinge on how we reconcile these two impulses: to engineer our way forward or to live within the planet’s boundaries.

books.title: The World in a Grain
books.summary: The World in a Grain shows how ordinary sand underpins modern civilization—forming the concrete, asphalt, glass, and silicon that make our cities, roads, windows, and smartphones—while revealing the hidden global supply chains, speculative booms, and criminal “sand mafias” that feed an insatiable construction and tech economy. Vince Beiser traces why not all sand is usable (desert grains are too rounded), how dredging and river mining erode coasts, ruin habitats, and worsen floods, and how land-reclamation megaprojects and urbanization in Asia and the Middle East drive explosive demand that outpaces regulation. He details the weak governance, corruption, and violence surrounding extraction; the geopolitical stakes of shifting shorelines; and the technical limits of substitutes (recycled aggregates, manufactured sand) without systemic reform. His conclusion is that sand scarcity is a slow-burn ecological and social crisis that requires stronger international standards, enforcement, and redesign of how we build.

books.title: The World's Largest Prime Number
books.summary: A novelty book that is exactly what its title promises—over four hundred pages filled with nothing but the digits of a record-breaking Mersenne prime, running to nearly twenty-five million digits. Conceived as a deadpan prank gift and coffee-table curiosity, it has a companion volume, The World's Smallest Prime Number, whose contents amount to the number 2.

books.title: The Worlds I See
books.summary: Fei-Fei Li’s deeply personal memoir chronicling her journey from a teenage immigrant facing financial hardship in suburban New Jersey to becoming one of the most influential figures in AI. The narrative intertwines her family’s struggle, academic perseverance—from Princeton to Caltech—to her breakthrough scientific innovation, ImageNet, which catalyzed the modern AI renaissance. Li shares how curiosity, mentorship, and resilience fueled her path, while also weaving in the intellectual and ethical challenges of AI—its promise, its dangers, and the critical need for human-centered design. Through candid stories of scientific discovery, her efforts in diversity (AI4All), and advocacy for aligning AI with human values, Li illuminates both how AI—and her own life—was shaped, and how each informs the other.

books.title: This Is How They Tell Me the World Ends
books.summary: This Is How They Tell Me the World Ends is an investigative account of the secretive global cyberweapons market, where governments, hackers, and private brokers buy and sell “zero-day” exploits—previously unknown software vulnerabilities that can be weaponized to infiltrate critical systems. Nicole Perlroth traces how U.S. intelligence agencies pioneered the stockpiling of such exploits, how the market expanded into a multibillion-dollar gray industry, and how rivals like Russia, China, North Korea, and Iran have caught up, escalating the risk of cyberwarfare. The book exposes how poorly regulated this trade remains, the dangers of state and corporate dependence on insecure systems, and how the hunt for digital advantage leaves the entire world vulnerable to catastrophic attacks on infrastructure, democracy, and personal security.

books.title: Tiananmen Square
books.summary:
The book argues that the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests were a pivotal moment in modern Chinese history, revealing the complexities of China's political system and the enduring legacy of the Communist Party's authoritarian rule.

The broad organisation of the book is as follows:
- Establishing the significance and complexity of the Tiananmen Square protests (Chapters 1-3)
- Highlighting the interplay between domestic and international factors (Chapter 4)
- Demonstrating the enduring legacy of the protests and the Communist Party's authoritarian rule (Chapter 5)

books.title: To Be Fair
books.summary: Fairness is a core human instinct—rooted in our neurology and evolution as a balance between competition and cooperation. This instinct shaped history and institutions before fraying in the twenty-first century amid financial shocks, culture wars, and technology-driven discourse. Ben Fenton defines what we really mean by fair play, shows how it operates across sport, business and economics, law and taxation, politics and government, communication and technology, and intimate relationships, and explains why violations of fairness feel viscerally wrong. The book’s case is that fairness functions as a social contract between people; when asymmetric power, opaque systems, or bad-faith communication corrode that contract, trust collapses.
