It concludes by urging the deliberate rebuilding of fair processes—clear rules, transparency, reciprocity, and civil discourse—so that shared standards of fair play can restore cooperation and social cohesion.

books.title: Tomorrow 3.0
books.summary: An economist's short, provocative take on the sharing economy, arguing that its real significance lies in the collapse of transaction costs. Munger predicts that platforms which make it cheap to rent rather than own will transform how we use goods, likening the coming shift to earlier revolutions in commerce and probing its consequences for work, ownership, and the welfare state.

books.title: Toward a Free Economy
books.summary: A history of economic ideas centred on the Swatantra Party, the free-market opposition that challenged Nehruvian planning in India from 1959 into the early 1970s. Balasubramanian recovers how a distinctively Indian economic conservatism took shape and spread within a democracy, mobilizing people around inflation, taxation, and property rights, and argues for the party's lasting influence on Indian political and economic thought.

books.title: Tribe
books.summary: Modern society, despite its wealth and safety, leaves people feeling isolated and disconnected compared to the deep bonds of small groups that humans evolved to live in. Drawing on anthropology, psychology, and his experiences as a war correspondent, Junger shows how traditional tribal communities and the intense solidarity of soldiers at war provide meaning, equality, and belonging, while modern life often fosters loneliness and division. He also examines how trauma and disaster can paradoxically bring people together, and why veterans struggle to reintegrate into individualistic societies. The book ultimately calls for rebuilding stronger communal ties as the foundation of resilience and fulfillment.

books.title: Turn Around Diabetes
books.summary: Turn Around Diabetes presents a step-by-step, evidence-based roadmap to reverse Type 2 diabetes and better manage Type 1 diabetes using sustainable lifestyle changes—with the goal of reducing medication, boosting energy, and improving overall health. Dr. Sanghani introduces the “Lifestyle Car” framework composed of four core pillars—nutrition, sleep, stress management, and exercise—to form the foundation of metabolic health, with optional use of intermittent fasting when appropriate. Drawing from hundreds of clinical studies, real patient examples, and the latest research, she structures the book to empower readers with practical tools and awareness extending beyond traditional medical care. The approach emphasises personalisation, holistic integration of mind, body, and spirit, and motivational interviewing techniques to help individuals take control of their diabetes journey and reclaim vitality.

books.title: Uncivil Agreement
books.summary: Uncivil Agreement explores how American political polarisation has deepened, not just because of policy disagreements, but because politics has become tied to people’s social and personal identities. Mason shows that over the past few decades, partisan divisions have increasingly overlapped with racial, religious, geographic, and cultural identities, creating what she calls “mega-identities.” This alignment means that political conflict now feels like an attack on one’s core self rather than just a debate over issues, leading to stronger partisan loyalty, hostility toward the other side, and less willingness to compromise. The book draws on political science research to explain how identity-driven polarisation has transformed American democracy into a more tribal and emotionally charged contest.

books.title: Us vs. Them
books.summary: Us vs Them examines the growing backlash against globalisation and how it has fueled populist politics worldwide. Bremmer argues that while globalisation lifted millions out of poverty and expanded trade, it also created sharp inequalities, left many communities behind, and eroded trust in elites and institutions. This discontent has manifested in nationalism, protectionism, and anti-immigrant sentiment, seen in movements like Brexit, Trump’s rise, and far-right politics in Europe. He explores how technology, migration, and economic dislocation have deepened divides between the beneficiaries of global integration and those excluded from it, warning that without reforms to make globalisation more inclusive, the trend toward populism and polarisation will only intensify.

books.title: Vajpayee - Believer's Dilemma
books.summary: This is the second half of Atal Bihari Vajpayee’s political life — from the late 1970s through his premiership into the rise of the Hindu Right. It explains how the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and its affiliates moved from the margins to the centre of Indian politics. Choudhary uses new archival material and interviews to trace Vajpayee’s role in key moments such as his coalition-building, nuclear tests, diplomatic pushes, the setbacks in the BJP’s secular image, and the strategy of the Sangh Parivar’s ascent. It argues that Vajpayee was both a bridge-figure and a strategist whose ambitions and ideological loyalties reflected the dilemmas of a nationalist movement entering state power. The book concludes that the real transformation in Indian politics was less about individuals than about shifting institutional alliances and ideologies, and that Vajpayee’s legacy must be read in the light of the Hindu Right’s consolidation rather than solely his own achievements.

books.title: Vajpayee - The Ascent of the Hindu Right
books.summary: The first volume of a two-part biography of Atal Bihari Vajpayee, covering 1924 to 1977—from his childhood and RSS beginnings through his emergence as the most acceptable public face of the Hindu right. Choudhary uses Vajpayee's life to trace the wider ascent of Hindu nationalism in independent India, in a richly researched and balanced account that won the Tata Literature Live! First Book Award.

books.title: Valley of Genius
books.summary: An oral history of Silicon Valley, told through the voices of the founders, engineers, investors, and cultural figures who built the modern tech world. Drawing on first-person accounts, it traces the Valley’s evolution from 1960s counterculture and hacker ethos through the rise of Apple, Atari, Pixar, Google, Facebook, and beyond. The narrative highlights both the eccentric, often rebellious personalities who drove innovation and the cultural clashes between idealism, creativity, and the relentless pursuit of profit. By letting the insiders speak directly, the book captures the messy, serendipitous, and chaotic nature of technological breakthroughs that reshaped the world.

books.title: Vienna
books.summary: A cultural and intellectual history arguing that an astonishing share of modern thought—from psychoanalysis and logical positivism to free-market economics, modern design, and management theory—was incubated in early twentieth-century Vienna. Cockett, an Economist editor, follows the city's thinkers from the ferment of Red Vienna through the catastrophe of fascism, showing how their dispersal across the world carried Viennese ideas into every corner of modern life.

books.title: Vishwa Shastra
books.summary: A comprehensive overview of India's engagement with the world from ancient times to the present, aimed especially at students and policymakers. Jaishankar traces early India's far-flung connections, the costs of colonialism, and the country's post-independence rivalries with Pakistan and China, charting its journey from Cold War non-alignment to contemporary realignment and laying out its core strategic objectives.

books.title: War
books.summary:
An in-depth look at the Biden administration focusing on the war in Ukraine, escalating tensions in the Middle East, and the political struggle between Trump and Biden for the American presidency. The book delves into President [[Joe Biden]]'s interactions with global leaders, including Russian President Vladimir Putin, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, highlighting the complexities of wartime diplomacy and the administration's efforts to prevent nuclear escalation. Additionally, it examines the domestic political landscape, focusing on the contentious dynamics between Biden and former President [[Donald Trump]] as the 2024 presidential election approaches.

He concludes that President [[Joe Biden]] and his administration exemplify "steady and purposeful leadership" based on their handling of the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East. Biden was cautious and deliberate about his foreign policy, emphasizing, at every step of the way, diplomacy and strategic restraint. Most particularly his aversion to deploying U.S. troops directly in conflict zones.

books.title: Ways of Remembering
books.summary: A scholarly study of how independent India remembers the 2002 Gujarat pogrom through the intertwined languages of law and cinema. Using a "jurisprudential aesthetic" method, Sircar reads the judgments in the Best Bakery case alongside three Bollywood films, arguing that both law and film shape a collective memory in which secular legal rationality is offered as the answer to religious violence.

books.title: We Are Bellingcat
books.summary: We Are Bellingcat tells the story of how a collective of citizen investigators, armed with open-source intelligence (OSINT) and digital tools, uncovered some of the most significant geopolitical events of the past decade. Higgins recounts how Bellingcat began as a one-person blog analysing YouTube videos of the Syrian conflict and grew into a global team that exposed the downing of Malaysia Airlines Flight MH17, traced chemical weapons use in Syria, and identified Russian intelligence agents involved in the Skripal poisoning. The book explains their methods—geolocation, metadata analysis, cross-referencing social media—and shows how transparency and collaborative investigation can challenge the monopoly of governments and intelligence agencies over truth. It also reflects on the risks of disinformation and the responsibility that comes with democratised investigative power.

books.title: We, the People of the States of Bharat
books.summary: A book that traces the evolution of India’s federal structure, showing how the Indian Union was shaped through historical processes, political compromises, and constitutional design. He examines the integration of princely states, the linguistic reorganization of states, and the continuing tensions between the Centre and the states over issues like resources, representation, and identity. Through historical narrative and case studies, Chopra highlights how India’s federalism has been both contested and adaptive, holding together extraordinary diversity while facing periodic challenges from secessionist movements, regional demands, and centralizing tendencies. The book ultimately underscores how India’s unity has depended on managing federal negotiations rather than enforcing uniformity.

books.title: Weapons of Math Destruction
books.summary: Weapons of Math Destruction is a critique of how big data algorithms, marketed as objective and scientific, often perpetuate inequality and injustice at scale. The book explains how predictive models used in areas like policing, education, hiring, credit scoring, and insurance rely on biased historical data, are opaque to those affected, and lack feedback mechanisms for correction. Because they are widespread, inscrutable, and consequential, these systems create self-reinforcing cycles of disadvantage—what O’Neil calls “weapons of math destruction.” She argues that while algorithms have potential for good, without accountability, transparency, and ethical design, they amplify discrimination and harm the very people they claim to serve.

books.title: What Just Happened
books.summary: A collection of Gleick's technology essays and columns, many drawn from his 1990s "Fast Forward" writing for The New York Times Magazine, chronicling the early digital revolution as it unfolded. Ranging over software bugs, the growth of the internet, privacy, and life in an "inescapably connected" world, the pieces form a prescient dispatch from the frontier of the information age.

books.title: When the Chips Are Down
books.summary: When the Chips Are Down explains how semiconductors have become a cornerstone of global geopolitical, geoeconomic and technological competition - for the first time from an India lens. The book explains how the chip-industry evolved: from its scientific roots, through economies like the U.S., Taiwan and Japan taking the lead, to the present moment where manufacturing is highly concentrated, supply-chains are fragile (highlighted by the COVID-19 shortages), and nations are scrambling to secure access and local capacity. It shows why countries such as India have so far lagged behind in chip manufacturing (despite hardware design strength), explores how export controls, investment subsidies and alliances are reshaping the industry, and outlines what might come next. The conclusion is that semiconductors are a “meta-critical” technology—embedded in everything we use—and that control over them will heavily influence economic power, national security and technological leadership.

books.title: Who Can You Trust
books.summary: Who Can You Trust? explores how trust, once anchored in traditional institutions like governments, banks, and media, is shifting in the digital age toward distributed networks, platforms, and peer-to-peer systems. Botsman traces the evolution of trust from local, community-based forms to institutional trust, and now to what she calls “distributed trust,” where people rely on strangers through platforms like Airbnb, Uber, and blockchain-based systems. She argues that while this new model can democratise trust and enable new forms of collaboration, it also brings risks—fragile reputations, opaque algorithms, and concentration of power in digital intermediaries—that demand new frameworks of accountability.

books.title: Who Owns This Sentence
books.summary: A global history of copyright that traces its evolution from eighteenth-century London to the age of Facebook and artificial intelligence. Bellos and Montagu argue that copyright, far from being a natural right, is a social construction that has expanded relentlessly to cover ever more of human creativity—and has become, in their telling, an engine of inequality in the modern economy.

books.title: Whole Numbers and Half Truths
books.summary: Whole Numbers and Half Truths is a data-driven exploration of contemporary India, showing how official statistics, surveys, and numbers can both illuminate and obscure the realities of Indian life. Drawing from years of work as a data journalist, the book tackles subjects ranging from population, caste, gender, inequality, employment, health, and religion to crime and electoral politics, revealing how the country’s vastness and diversity often make neat numerical conclusions misleading. It explains how data is collected, the biases built into official surveys, and the gaps between what numbers suggest and what lived experiences reveal, ultimately urging readers to treat data neither as absolute truth nor as meaningless, but as a lens that requires careful interpretation.

books.title: Why Europe Grew Rich and Asia Did Not
books.summary: Why Europe Grew Rich and Asia Did Not challenges the conventional narrative that Europe’s economic rise was inevitable due to superior institutions, culture, or innovation. Using comparative data from India, China, and Europe in the 18th century, he shows that Asian economies were in many respects as advanced as Europe’s, with competitive textile industries, skilled labor, and complex markets. The key divergence, he argues, came from Europe’s access to abundant coal and colonies, which allowed it to escape resource constraints and finance industrial growth, while Asian regions—lacking such external advantages and facing colonial exploitation—were constrained despite comparable capabilities. The book reframes industrialization not as a product of European exceptionalism but as the contingent outcome of ecological resources and imperial power.

books.title: Why Fish Dont Exist
books.summary: Why Fish Don’t Exist blends memoir, biography, and philosophy to tell the story of taxonomist David Starr Jordan, who devoted his life to classifying species and reorganizing the natural world, even as chaos—from earthquakes destroying his specimens to the exposure of his ties to eugenics—undermined his work. Through his life, Miller examines the human impulse to impose order on nature and our own lives, questioning whether classification provides stability or blinds us to reality. Interwoven with her personal struggles and reflections, the book challenges the very category of “fish,” showing how scientific classifications are human constructs that can collapse under scrutiny. In the end, it suggests that embracing uncertainty and chaos, rather than denying them, is a more honest and resilient way to live.

books.title: Why Machines Learn
books.summary:
An exploration of the mathematics and theories that underpin modern machine learning and artificial intelligence. Ananthaswamy traces the history of machine learning, the key breakthroughs and the brilliant minds behind them. From early attempts at pattern recognition to the advent of neural networks and deep learning, the book charts the field’s rapid evolution. He explores how mathematics provides the foundation for these advancements, focusing on concepts such as linear algebra, calculus, probability, and optimization.

The book examines specific techniques that power AI systems, such as gradient descent, back-propagation, and the use of large datasets for training models. Through these explanations, Ananthaswamy reveals how machines develop the ability to recognize patterns, make decisions, and even generate creative outputs. The book probes the connections between artificial intelligence and human cognition, asking whether the way machines "learn" mirrors how humans acquire knowledge. It also addresses the ethical challenges posed by AI, such as bias in algorithms, privacy concerns, and the potential for misuse.

books.title: Why We Die
books.summary: Venki Ramakrishnan’s Why We Die explains death as the breakdown of the body’s ability to function as a whole, caused by cumulative cellular and molecular failures such as DNA damage, telomere shortening, mitochondrial decline, and protein misfolding. He situates ageing within evolutionary trade-offs, showing how genes that improve reproduction early in life contribute to deterioration later. The book surveys current scientific attempts to slow or reverse ageing—drugs like rapamycin, manipulation of epigenetics, telomere extension, and metabolic interventions—while pointing out their limits and risks, including cancer and unforeseen side effects. Ramakrishnan also critiques the anti-ageing industry and transhumanist promises of radical life extension, arguing that most claims are exaggerated. He concludes that while science may modestly extend healthy lifespan, the only proven ways to live longer and better today are maintaining good sleep, diet, and exercise, and that society must carefully weigh the ethical and social consequences of any future interventions.

books.title: Why the Poor Don’t Kill Us
books.summary: A very enjoyable, sometimes hilarious, read about how the poor in India are really quite unbelievably tolerant. That given the dramatic social disparities it is truly a wonder that they haven't revolted yet. Full of reflections and observations about our country and the way we live.

books.title: Word Perfect
books.summary: A linguistic almanac offering a morsel of etymological delight for every day of the year, from the lexicographer best known as the resident word expert on Countdown's Dictionary Corner. Dent unearths the surprising origins of everyday phrases and revives forgotten or oddly useful words—like "tartle," the panic of forgetting someone's name just as you must introduce them.

books.title: Working in Public
books.summary: Working in Public examines the culture and economics of open source software, shifting the focus from creation to maintenance. Nadia Eghbal argues that while open source was once built around communities of contributors, today’s projects often resemble creator-driven platforms where a small number of maintainers do the bulk of the work while millions consume the output. She classifies projects into models—stadiums (few creators, many consumers), clubs (closed, collaborative), federations (distributed networks), and toy projects (small and personal)—to illustrate how attention and participation shape sustainability. The book highlights the hidden labour of maintainers—triaging issues, writing documentation, managing users—that is undervalued compared to new code. Eghbal connects these dynamics to the broader “economy of attention” in online platforms, arguing that maintaining digital infrastructure requires rethinking incentives, funding, and recognition.

books.title: Your Face Belongs to Us
books.summary: Your Face Belongs to Us chronicles the rise of Clearview AI—a small, secretive startup that scraped billions of publicly available photos from the internet to build a facial recognition tool it sold to law enforcement, billionaires, and businesses. Hill traces Clearview’s origins in Silicon Valley, the controversial figures who backed it, and how it pushed this powerful surveillance tool into use despite major tech firms like Google and Facebook deciding such capabilities were too risky to release. The book outlines how this unlocked surveillance capability enabled wrongful arrests, amplified global authoritarian reach, and exposed deep biases within AI systems. Hill highlights efforts in parts of Europe to ban or fine the technology while contrasting that with the United States’ fragmented legal protections. She concludes with a stark warning: this technology may be impossible to stop, and without regulation or public awareness, the erosion of anonymity and privacy is not a dystopian possibility—it’s already here.

books.title: Zealot
books.summary: Reza Aslan writes about Christ as a normal human and a jew and in this book tries to paint him as a sort of a terrorist of that time. He alleges that the crime he committed in Roman eyes was akin to treason and revolt as he instigated an uprising against the ruling class. This is a remarkable attempt at humanising the religion - but one that is unlikely to go down well with the religious.
